title: [Rule] Amendments to the “Small Business” and “Small Organization” Definitions for Investment Companies and Investment Advisers for Purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act
abstract: The Securities and Exchange Commission (the "Commission" or the "SEC") is amending the definitions of "small business" and "small organization" (collectively, "small entities") that are used in connection with Commission rulemaking under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (the "Investment Company Act") and the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (the "Advisers Act"). These definitions concern regulatory requirements applicable to registered investment companies and business development companies (collectively, "funds") as well as investment advisers. The definitions are used specifically for purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (the "RFA"), which requires the Commission to consider the impact of its regulations on small entities. The amendments are designed to modernize the definitions, by increasing certain asset-based thresholds, including a mechanism for periodic future inflation adjustments, and eliminating the threshold based on total assets for advisers. In connection with these amendments, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV as well as the rule that allows certain small SEC-registered advisers to apply for a continuing hardship exemption from making Advisers Act filings electronically.

[Release Nos. IA-7035; IC-36380; File No. S7-2026-01]

Amendments to the ``Small Business'' and ``Small Organization'' 
Definitions for Investment Companies and Investment Advisers for 
Purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act

AGENCY: Securities and Exchange Commission.

ACTION: Final rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Securities and Exchange Commission (the ``Commission'' or 
the ``SEC'') is amending the definitions of ``small business'' and 
``small organization'' (collectively, ``small entities'') that are used 
in connection with Commission rulemaking under the Investment Company 
Act of 1940 (the ``Investment Company Act'') and the Investment 
Advisers Act of 1940 (the ``Advisers Act''). These definitions concern 
regulatory requirements applicable to registered investment companies 
and business development companies (collectively, ``funds'') as well as 
investment advisers. The definitions are used specifically for purposes 
of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (the ``RFA''), which requires the 
Commission to consider the impact of its regulations on small entities. 
The amendments are designed to modernize the definitions, by increasing 
certain asset-based thresholds, including a mechanism for periodic 
future inflation adjustments, and eliminating the threshold based on 
total assets for advisers. In connection with these amendments, the 
Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV as well as the 
rule that allows certain small SEC-registered advisers to apply for a 
continuing hardship exemption from making Advisers Act filings 
electronically.

DATES: This final rule was published in the Federal Register on 
November 6, 2026.
     Final amendments to 17 CFR 270.0-10 (``rule 0-10'') and 17 
CFR 275.0-7 (``rule 0-7'') are effective February 4, 2027.
     Final amendments to 17 CFR 275.203-3 (``rule 203-3'') and 
17 CFR 279.1 (``Form ADV'') are effective, and have a compliance date 
of, February 4, 2027.

I. Introduction

    We are adopting amendments to Commission rules that define a 
``small entity'' under the RFA for funds and investment advisers by 
raising the asset thresholds contained in both definitions.\3\ 
Specifically, the amendments to the Investment Company Act rule (rule 
0-10) will increase the net asset threshold for

[[Page 69956]]

funds to be considered ``small'' from $50 million to $10 billion and 
replace the ``group of related investment companies'' definition in the 
rule with ``family of investment companies,'' as that term is currently 
used in Form N-CEN. We are also adopting amendments to the Advisers Act 
rule (rule 0-7) that will increase the amount of regulatory assets 
under management (``RAUM'') below which an adviser is considered small 
from $25 million to $1 billion, eliminate the $5 million total assets 
threshold provision from the definition, and make conforming amendments 
to the adviser control relationship threshold to reflect the increased 
adviser RAUM threshold in the definition. Additionally, the amendments 
to Investment Company Act rule 0-10 and Advisers Act rule 0-7 will 
provide a mechanism for future inflation adjustments to the thresholds. 
Finally, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV and 
Advisers Act rule 203-3(b) for hardship exemptions to implement the 
amended adviser RAUM threshold. The final rules reflect comments the 
Commission received on amendments it proposed in January 2026 and will 
help the Commission more appropriately promote the effectiveness and 
efficiency of its regulations, with the goal of minimizing significant 
economic impact on small entities, consistent with the RFA.\4\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \3\ Unless otherwise specified, the term ``investment 
companies'' or ``funds'' in this release refers collectively to 
registered investment companies and business development companies 
but not entities excluded from the definition of investment company 
under the Investment Company Act such as private funds.
    \4\ See Amendments to the ``Small Business'' and ``Small 
Organization'' Definitions for Investment Companies and Investment 
Advisers for Purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act, Investment 
Company Act Release No. 35864 (Jan. 7, 2026) [91 FR 1107 (Jan. 12, 
2026)] (the ``Proposing Release''). The comment letters on the 
Proposing Release (File No. S7-2026-01) are available at https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/public-comments/s7-2026-01. See also 
Enhancement of Emerging Growth Company Accommodations and 
Simplification of Filer Status for Reporting Companies, Release No. 
33-11419 (May 19, 2026) [91 FR 30086 (May 21, 2026)] (``2026 Filer 
Status Release'') (among other things, proposing amendments to the 
``small entity'' definitions for purposes of the Securities Act of 
1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the ``Exchange 
Act'')).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Background

    The Commission has a longstanding commitment to understanding and 
addressing the concerns of small entities and has established the 
Office of Small Business Policy in the Division of Corporation Finance, 
the Office of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation, and 
the Small Business Capital Formation Advisory Committee to be 
responsive to such concerns.\5\ In the context of rulemaking, the 
Commission tailors its regulations to the relevant characteristics of 
regulated entities and weighs the impact of its rules on small 
entities, including through performing analyses under the RFA.\6\ A 
purpose of the RFA is to promote the effectiveness and efficiency of 
regulations, including through consideration of alternative regulatory 
approaches, with the goal of minimizing the significant economic impact 
on small entities consistent with the stated objectives of applicable 
statutes.\7\ The Commission is required to determine if a rulemaking is 
likely to have a ``significant economic impact on a substantial number 
of small entities'' under the RFA.\8\ Unless the Commission certifies 
that the rulemaking will not have such an impact, the Commission is 
required to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis both during the 
proposal and final stages of adopting a rule.\9\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \5\ See Proposing Release, at n.1 (discussing the history of 
these Commission offices and the committee).
    \6\ See Proposing Release, at section I.A.1.
    \7\ Public Law 96-354, 2, Sept. 19, 1980, 94 Stat. 1164; 5 
U.S.C. 601-612.
    \8\ See 5 U.S.C. 605(b). The RFA does not define ``significant 
economic impact'' or ``substantial number of small entities.''
    \9\ See 5 U.S.C. 603-604; see also 5 U.S.C. 605(b).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The Small Business Act gives the Administrator of the U.S. Small 
Business Administration (the ``SBA'') authority to establish small 
business size standards for all Federal agencies, in the absence of 
other specific statutory authority.\10\ An agency may nevertheless 
prescribe its own small business size standard pursuant to section 
601(3) of the RFA if, as described in 13 CFR 121.903(c), the agency 
consults with the SBA Office of Advocacy and the size standard will be 
used for the sole purpose of performing an RFA analysis.\11\ Allowing 
agencies to establish their own definitions for the terms ``small 
business,'' ``small organization,'' and ``small governmental 
jurisdiction'' for purposes of the RFA analyses gives agencies 
flexibility in applying the provisions of the RFA.\12\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \10\ 15 U.S.C. 632(a)(2). 15 U.S.C. 632(a)(1) sets forth the 
default standard for a ``small business concern'' as ``one which is 
independently owned and operated and which is not dominant in its 
field of operation.''
    \11\ 13 CFR 121.903(c); see also Small Business Size 
Regulations; Size Standards for Programs of Other Agencies, 67 FR 
13714 (Mar. 26, 2002).
    \12\ 5 U.S.C. 601. Under the RFA, the term ``small entity'' has 
the same meaning as the terms ``small business,'' ``small 
organization,'' and ``small governmental jurisdiction'' as defined 
under the RFA, unless the agency has established a definition of 
such term. In the latter case, the definition of the term is instead 
what was established by the agency.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In 1982, the Commission adopted rule 0-10 for investment companies 
and rule 0-7 for investment advisers to define ``small business'' and 
``small organization'' for purposes of Commission rulemakings under the 
Investment Company Act and Advisers Act, respectively.\13\ These 
definitions were last amended in 1998 \14\ and, in connection with 
outreach to small entities, the Commission has subsequently received 
requests to update the definitions.\15\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \13\ See Final Definitions of ``Small Business'' and ``Small 
Organization'' for Purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act, 
Investment Company Act Release No. 12194 (Jan. 28, 1982) [47 FR 5215 
(Feb. 4, 1982)] (``1982 Adopting Release''); see also Proposing 
Release, at section I.A.2 and I.A.3 (explaining the history of the 
Commission's investment company and investment adviser size 
standards).
    \14\ See Definitions of ``Small Business'' or ``Small 
Organization'' Under the Investment Company Act of 1940, Investment 
Advisers Act of 1940, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and the 
Securities Act of 1933, Investment Company Act Release No. 23272 
(June 24, 1998) [63 FR 35508 (June 30, 1998)] (``1998 Adopting 
Release'').
    \15\ See Proposing Release, at n.10.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Under rule 0-10, an investment company is deemed a small entity if 
it, together with other investment companies in the same group of 
related investment companies, has net assets of $50 million or less as 
of the end of its most recent fiscal year.\16\ A group of related 
investment companies is defined, with respect to management companies, 
as two or more management companies (including series thereof) that (i) 
hold themselves out to investors as related companies for purposes of 
investment and investor services; and (ii) either (1) have a common 
investment adviser or have investment advisers that are affiliated 
persons of each other; or (2) have a common administrator.\17\ Under 
rule 0-7, an investment adviser is deemed a small entity if it: (i) has 
RAUM \18\ of less than $25 million (the ``RAUM Threshold''); \19\ (ii) 
did not have total assets \20\ of $5 million or more on the last day of 
the most recent fiscal year (the ``Total Assets Threshold''); and (iii) 
does not control, is not controlled by, and is not under common control 
with (a ``control relationship'') another investment adviser that has 
assets under management of $25 million or more, or

[[Page 69957]]

any person (other than a natural person) that had total assets of $5 
million or more on the last day of the most recent fiscal year (the 
``Control Relationship Threshold'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \16\ See 17 CFR 210.6-04 (Regulation S-X section generally 
applicable to balance sheets filed by registered investment 
companies and business development companies, including requirements 
for disclosure of net assets).
    \17\ 17 CFR 270.0-10(a). In the case of unit investment trusts 
(``UITs''), a group of related investment companies is defined as 
two or more UITs (including series thereof) that have a common 
sponsor.
    \18\ RAUM are securities portfolios for which the adviser 
provides continuous and regular supervisory or management services. 
See Form ADV, Instructions for Part 1A, Instruction 5(b).
    \19\ See Proposing Release, at n.11 (discussing the basis for 
the use of the term ``regulatory assets under management'').
    \20\ See 17 CFR 275.0-7(b)(2); 1998 Adopting Release at n.42 
(describing ``total assets'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In January 2026, the Commission proposed amendments to the 
investment company and investment adviser ``small entity'' definitions. 
Specifically, the Commission proposed to:
     Amend rule 0-10 for funds to: (i) increase the net asset 
threshold for funds from $50 million to $10 billion; and (ii) refer, 
for purposes of aggregating the net assets of related funds, to a 
``family of investment companies'' as that term is used in Item B.5 of 
Form N-CEN rather than to a ``group of related investment companies'' 
as used in the current rule;
     Amend rule 0-7 for investment advisers to increase the 
RAUM Threshold below which an investment adviser is considered to be a 
``small entity'' from $25 million to $1 billion and to conform the 
assets under management threshold in the Control Relationship Threshold 
with the revisions made to the RAUM Threshold;
     Amend Form ADV to revise the instructions and Item 12 of 
Part 1A of Form ADV, including through making conforming changes to 
Form ADV, and amend rule 203-3 providing a continuing hardship 
exemption from electronic filing requirements; and
     Amend rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 to allow the Commission to 
make subsequent inflation adjustments to the asset thresholds in these 
rules by order every 10 years in accordance with an inflation 
adjustment mechanism.
    The Commission also requested comment on whether to amend the Total 
Assets Threshold, as well as the total assets threshold contained in 
the Control Relationship Threshold, in rule 0-7.
    The Commission received approximately 20 comments on the proposed 
amendments. Commenters generally supported the proposal's goal to 
modernize the ``small entity'' definitions.\21\ These commenters noted 
that the current rules are out of date and stated that the proposed 
amendments would help calibrate the Commission's analysis of the 
regulatory and compliance costs for small entities under the RFA.\22\ 
Some commenters suggested modifications to the proposal, such as a 
higher fund net asset threshold, alternative non-RAUM Thresholds, 
different mechanisms for future threshold adjustments, elimination of 
the adviser Total Assets Threshold, or different treatment of certain 
entities.\23\ Some commenters expressed concern that the proposal would 
diminish investor protections and suggested lower asset thresholds.\24\ 
After consideration of the comments received, and as discussed in more 
detail below, the Commission is adopting the amendments largely as 
proposed but with some modifications in response to comments.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \21\ See, e.g., Comment Letter of the Investment Company 
Institute (Mar. 13, 2026) (``ICI Comment Letter''); Comment Letter 
of MFA (Mar. 13, 2026) (``MFA Comment Letter''); Comment Letter of 
the Independent Directors Council (Mar. 13, 2026) (``IDC Comment 
Letter'').
    \22\ See, e.g., Comment Letter of the National Venture Capital 
Association (Mar. 11, 2026) (``NVCA Comment Letter''); Comment 
Letter of the Small Business Investor Alliance (Mar. 16, 2026) 
(``SBIA Comment Letter'').
    \23\ See, e.g., ICI Comment Letter; Comment Letter of Proskauer 
Rose LLP (Mar. 13, 2026) (``Proskauer Comment Letter''); Comment 
Letter of the Committee of Annuity Insurers (Mar. 10, 2026) (``CAI 
Comment Letter'').
    \24\ See, e.g., Comment Letter of the Public Investors Advocate 
Bar Association (Mar. 16, 2026) (``PIABA Comment Letter''); Comment 
Letter of Better Markets (Mar. 13, 2026) (``Better Markets Comment 
Letter'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

B. Overview of the Final Amendments

    We are amending the definitions of ``small business'' and ``small 
organization'' under the Investment Company Act and the Advisers Act 
for purposes of the RFA, largely as proposed, but with modifications:
     Raising the Fund Net Asset Threshold. As proposed, the 
Commission is raising the net asset threshold for funds from $50 
million to $10 billion.\25\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \25\ Final 17 CFR 270.0-10.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     Amending the Fund Group Definition. As proposed, the 
Commission is, for purposes of aggregating the net assets of related 
funds, replacing the term ``group of related investment companies'' 
with ``family of investment companies'' as that term is used in Item 
B.5 of Form N-CEN.
     Raising the Adviser RAUM Threshold. As proposed, the 
Commission is raising the RAUM Threshold from $25 million to $1 
billion, and making conforming amendments to the Control Relationship 
Threshold to reflect the increased RAUM Threshold.\26\ In a change from 
the proposal, the Commission is amending the Control Relationship 
Threshold to help advisers understand how to calculate the threshold.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \26\ Final 17 CFR 275.0-7.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     Eliminating the Adviser Total Assets Threshold. In a 
change from the proposal, the Commission is eliminating the $5 million 
Total Assets Threshold, and making conforming amendments to the Control 
Relationship Threshold to reflect that the Commission is eliminating 
the Total Assets Threshold.
     Periodic Inflation Adjustments. As proposed, the 
Commission is amending rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 to allow the Commission 
to make subsequent inflation adjustments to the asset thresholds by 
order every 10 years in accordance with the inflation adjustment 
mechanism set forth in section II.C below (the ``Inflation Adjustment 
Mechanism'').
     Conforming Amendments to Form ADV and the Hardship 
Exemption Rule. As proposed, the Commission is making conforming 
amendments to Form ADV, the uniform application for investment adviser 
registration and report form by exempt reporting advisers, and rule 
203-3(b), which sets forth conditions for certain small SEC-registered 
advisers to apply for a continuing hardship exemption from the 
requirement to make Advisers Act filings electronically with the 
Investment Adviser Registration Depository (the ``IARD'').\27\ The 
amendments are designed to reflect the Commission's amendments to the 
RAUM Threshold, the Control Relationship Threshold, and their 
corresponding periodic Inflation Adjustment Mechanism. In a change from 
the proposal, the Commission is also making additional conforming 
amendments to Form ADV and rule 203-3(b) to reflect the determination 
at adoption to eliminate the Total Assets Threshold.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \27\ See infra footnote 127, and accompanying text (defining 
``exempt reporting advisers'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Smaller firms play an important role in the asset management 
industry.\28\ We are mindful that smaller firms may face 
disproportionate compliance burdens compared to larger firms.\29\ For 
example, compliance costs--such as staff time, recordkeeping, 
cybersecurity costs, and reliance on outside expertise or market data--
often do not scale with firm size,\30\ and have increased, while client 
fees have decreased.\31\ We also are mindful that failure to consider 
the impact of regulations on small entities could risk reducing 
innovation, competitiveness, and new market

[[Page 69958]]

participants.\32\ The Commission tailors its regulations to the 
relevant characteristics of regulated entities and weighs the impact of 
its rules on small entities, including through performing regulatory 
flexibility analysis under the RFA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \28\ Commenters agreed and stated, for example, that smaller 
funds offer innovation, and smaller advisers employ diverse 
investment philosophies and portfolio construction approaches, which 
broadens investor choice. See, e.g., ICI Comment Letter.
    \29\ See, e.g., Comment Letter of the Investment Adviser 
Association (Mar. 13, 2026) (``IAA Comment Letter'').
    \30\ See, e.g., MFA Comment Letter.
    \31\ See, e.g., Comment Letter of Garcia Hamilton & Associates, 
L.P. (Mar. 12, 2026) (``Garcia Hamilton Comment Letter'').
    \32\ See, e.g., Comment Letter of the CFP Board, Financial 
Planning Association, et al. (Mar. 13, 2026) (``CFP Board Comment 
Letter'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The final amendments are designed to help ensure the Commission's 
RFA analyses capture a more meaningful population of ``small entities'' 
so the Commission can continue to address the special concerns of small 
businesses. Updating the definitions of ``small business'' and ``small 
organization'' is appropriate to reflect the substantial growth in, and 
distribution of, regulatory assets under management and net assets over 
the decades since these thresholds were set.\33\ The updates to the 
definitions reflect more reliable and consistent metrics for whether an 
adviser or fund is small, compared to those in the current rules.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \33\ See infra section II.A.1 and section II.B.1.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Some commenters stated that the proposed amendments would classify 
too many funds or advisers as small (effectively leading the Commission 
to prioritize benefits of large funds and advisers instead of truly 
small funds and advisers),\34\ or otherwise could result in regulatory 
arbitrage between investment advisers and broker-dealers \35\ and 
diminish investor protections.\36\ As explained below, the final 
amendments will not classify too many funds or advisers as small. The 
final amendments also will not diminish investor protections. 
Designating an entity as a small entity does not reduce investor 
protection. Investor protection is a concern regardless of the size of 
an entity. The purpose of the small entity definition is, in part, to 
ensure that the Commission considers whether its rules are 
appropriately calibrated so that smaller entities are not subject to 
regulations that may be disproportionately burdensome relative to the 
benefits or improvements in investor protection. The final amendments 
will enhance the Commission's rulemaking process by helping ensure the 
RFA analyses reflect current economic realities by incorporating the 
evolution of adviser and fund growth since the rules were first 
adopted, as other commenters stated.\37\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \34\ See, e.g., PIABA Comment Letter.
    \35\ Comment Letter of the Securities Industry and Financial 
Markets Association (Mar. 13, 2026) (``SIFMA Comment Letter'') 
(noting the differences between the regulatory frameworks applicable 
to broker-dealers and investment advisers and stating that 
regulatory arbitrage is a contributing factor driving the shift from 
broker-dealer to registered investment adviser frameworks).
    \36\ PIABA Comment Letter.
    \37\ See e.g., IAA Comment Letter. One commenter expressed 
concern that the proposal would be inconsistent with an Executive 
Order and other Federal efforts to make housing affordable. This 
commenter expressed concern that reclassifying billion-dollar 
advisers and multi-billion-dollar fund families as ``small'' for 
securities rulemaking works at cross purposes with efforts to curb 
large institutional purchases of single-family homes. See Comment 
Letter of Angela Dowell (Feb. 26, 2026) (``Dowell Comment Letter'') 
(citing, for example, ``Stopping Wall Street From Competing with 
Main Street Homebuyers,'' Donald J. Trump Executive Order, Jan. 20, 
2026, available at https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/01/stopping-wall-street-from-competing-with-main-street-homebuyers/). We disagree that the final amendments will be 
inconsistent with the Executive Order or other Federal efforts to 
make housing affordable. The plain language of the current and final 
rules limits the application of the definitions, stating that the 
definitions of ``small business'' and ``small organization'' are for 
purposes of Commission rulemaking in accordance with the provisions 
of Chapter Six of the Administrative Procedure Act, unless otherwise 
defined for purposes of a particular rulemaking.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    One commenter stated that the proposal did not appear to evaluate 
the investor-protection consequences of the proposed amendments and 
asserted the proposal focused primarily on industry size, rather than 
regulatory risk or compliance capacity. It outlined certain areas that 
the Commission should quantify and analyze in this regard, in 
particular to focus any regulatory relief on genuinely small entities 
and in a risk-based manner.\38\ Because the final amendments primarily 
affect the process by which the Commission considers potential impacts 
on small entities, including benefits and costs of future rulemaking on 
small entities, the final amendments will not have any immediate impact 
on investor protection. Rather, the final amendments will require the 
Commission to consider and address the potential impacts of future 
rulemaking on small entities, including effects on investor protection.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \38\ Comment Letter of James E. Scarborough (Mar. 12, 2026) 
(``Scarborough Comment Letter'') (requesting analysis of investor 
exposure, regulatory relief consequences, risk-based threshold 
alternatives, and regulatory gap risk).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Separately, the methodology for the proposed thresholds reflects 
that advisory fees are generally scaled with an adviser's assets under 
management, where greater advisory fees can support an increased 
compliance capacity. The updated thresholds also will allow the 
Commission to more appropriately address in future rulemakings, in a 
risk-based manner, concerns that are unique to those entities that 
should be deemed small entities in view of the growth in assets since 
the rules were adopted and the appropriateness of any regulatory 
accommodations that may be provided to small entities.
    While conducting RFA analyses in future rulemakings, the Commission 
can take into account any potential for regulatory arbitrage between 
broker-dealers and investment advisers and adjust its future rules 
accordingly. The Commission carefully weighs the economic impact of its 
rules on all regulated entities, including small businesses, and 
tailors its regulations to the relevant characteristics of the 
particular entities regulated. In this way, the Commission works to 
meet its mandate under the Federal securities laws while at the same 
time considering any potentially disproportionate costs and regulatory 
burdens for small entities. The Commission intends to continue this 
careful, measured regulation that addresses small business concerns 
within the protections of the Federal securities laws.

II. Discussion

A. Amendments to Rule 0-10 Under the Investment Company Act

1. Raising the Net Asset Threshold
    The Commission is amending the net asset threshold for small funds, 
as proposed. The final rule will amend paragraph (a) of rule 0-10 to 
increase the net asset threshold from $50 million to $10 billion and, 
as discussed in more detail in section II.C below, establish a 
mechanism to inflation-adjust this figure every ten years. The increase 
accounts for the overall growth in the fund industry since the $50 
million threshold was originally set in 1982.\39\ At that time, 62.4% 
of funds were deemed ``small entities,'' but by 2024, the share of 
funds deemed ``small entities'' had fallen to 0.6%.\40\ Raising the net 
asset threshold in rule 0-10 to reflect growth in the investment 
company industry over the past decades will improve the utility of RFA 
analyses by more closely reflecting the population of funds that does 
not have the same competitive advantages as larger fund families (for 
instance, due to economies of scale when these larger families perform 
certain compliance and other operational functions in-house).\41\ It 
also will more closely reflect the population of funds that does not 
have the same negotiating power as larger

[[Page 69959]]

fund families when retaining service providers to perform compliance 
and operational functions.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \39\ See Proposing Release, at nn.50-55 and accompanying text.
    \40\ See 1982 Adopting Release; Proposing Release, at n.55 (85 
small entities/13,630 total registered investment companies and BDCs 
= 0.6%).
    \41\ Unless stated otherwise, the use of the term ``fund 
family'' or ``fund families'' in this release has the same meaning 
as ``family of investment companies.''
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In determining how to calibrate the amended threshold, the 
Commission considered the distribution of assets across individual 
funds and fund families, with the goal of ensuring that the proportion 
of funds that may face greater challenges in complying with Commission 
regulations due to their size be included in the small entity 
definition. Specifically, the Commission analyzed data reported on Form 
N-CEN to sort families of investment companies into percentiles 
according to their cumulative average total net assets. The Commission 
further analyzed this data to determine the percentage of individual 
funds and the percentage of average total net assets represented by 
each percentile.\42\ At proposal, the Commission estimated that, as of 
December 2024, fund families at or below the 80th percentile threshold 
of $10.04 billion in net assets accounted for 22.91% of individual 
funds and only 2.13% of fund assets.\43\ The analysis that formed the 
basis for the proposed threshold reflects that the assets of the 
investment company industry are heavily concentrated at the largest 
fund families, and these largest fund families not only manage a large 
majority of assets in the industry, but also account for a majority of 
the individual funds.\44\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \42\ See Proposing Release, at section II.A.1.
    \43\ See Proposing Release, at n.60; Table 1 and accompanying

    After considering these comments, we are, as proposed, raising the 
net asset threshold to $10 billion for funds. We agree with commenters' 
statements that the increased threshold would better reflect the growth 
in the fund industry and aid the Commission's analysis of regulatory 
and compliance costs on small funds.\51\ Based on analysis of the 
distribution of data discussed above, we are adopting a ``small 
entity'' definition that incorporates a $10 billion net asset 
threshold, which continues to correspond to the 80th percentile 
threshold in that distribution-based analysis.\52\ While the amended 
threshold will deem some relatively large individual funds ``small'' 
for purposes of the RFA, such an outcome is consistent with the 
economies of scale rationale for aggregating funds within a family. A 
single large fund with no other related funds will bear similar 
regulatory costs to several smaller, related funds that collectively 
represent a similar level of net assets. Therefore, aggregating assets 
across fund families reflects the Commission's understanding that funds 
within a complex typically use the same administrative, management, and 
compliance systems to oversee all the funds within the complex, so fees 
imposed on the fund by the adviser or administrator typically reflect 
economies of scale that the adviser or administrator achieves from 
managing other funds.

    While the Commission seeks to ensure that funds and fund families 
that may face greater challenges with regulatory compliance due to 
their size be deemed small entities, we are also mindful that setting 
the threshold too high has the potential to be counterproductive and to 
undermine the purpose of the Commission's RFA analyses. A higher 
threshold would result in a larger pool of small entities and therefore 
would increase the number of small entities needed to be affected by a 
rule for the rule to ``have a significant economic impact on a 
substantial number of small entities,'' which could lead to fewer RFA 
analyses being performed.\53\ Setting the threshold too high might also 
inadvertently lead to the Commission overlooking issues that concern 
the smallest entities when the Commission attempts to tailor its rules, 
and instead focusing primarily on issues of more general concern to the 
industry. Such an outcome might have the potential to perpetuate larger 
funds' advantages in the market, to the detriment of the smaller funds 
that the RFA was designed to protect.\54\ Accordingly, the Commission's 
amended threshold is meant to identify a level below which a meaningful 
proportion of funds would be deemed small entities, but above which the 
size of, and concentration of assets in, fund families increases to 
such an extent that treating individual funds within those families as 
small entities would not be consistent with the goals of the RFA. We 
are therefore not adopting a smaller threshold than the proposed $10 
billion threshold. We are also therefore not adopting a threshold of 
$12 billion as one commenter suggested. We do not believe this change 
from the proposed

the proposed threshold was designed to be stable and flexible enough to 
guide Commission analysis for the next 10 years and not to reflect 
short-term market fluctuations.

of related investment companies'' with ``family of investment 
companies,'' as that term is used in Item B.5 of Form N-CEN.\60\

B. Amendments To Rule 0-7 Under the Advisers Act

1. The RAUM Threshold
    As proposed, the final amendments will raise the RAUM Threshold 
from $25 million to $1 billion and add the Inflation Adjustment 
Mechanism.\69\ Rule 0-7 currently provides that an adviser is a small 
entity if it has assets under management of less than $25 million ``or 
such higher amount as the Commission may by rule deem appropriate under 
Section 203A(a)(1)(A) of the Act.'' \70\ As proposed, the final 
amendments remove the phrase ``or such higher amount as the Commission 
may by rule deem appropriate under Section 203A(a)(1)(A) of the Act (15 
U.S.C. 80b-3a(a)(1)(A)).'' \71\ The final amendments are designed to 
update the RAUM Threshold to reflect the growth of advisers' assets 
under management over time.\72\

    In contrast, a non-RAUM-based threshold would not be as reliable a 
metric to determine whether an adviser is small for RFA purposes as an 
RAUM-based threshold. An employee-based standard raises implementation 
challenges in appropriately addressing the use of service providers and 
outsourcing by investment advisers, which could distort the extent to 
which the number of an adviser's own employees reflects its actual 
resources and size. A commenter agreed, stating that an employee-based 
metric would penalize operational efficiency and outsourcing.\84\ This 
commenter cautioned that moving to an employee-based metric would 
incentivize the misclassification of staff as contractors to maintain 
``small entity'' status. Similarly, a threshold based on the number of 
clients or non-accredited investors also would not necessarily reflect 
an adviser's ability to devote resources towards compliance.\85\ For 
example, while an adviser could have only one fund as a client, that 
fund could be large both by RAUM and number of investors resulting in 
the adviser maintaining the capacity to devote significant resources 
towards compliance-related matters. Conversely, an adviser may have a 
large number of clients, but those clients' assets could represent a 
small amount of RAUM, so that the adviser would not have economies of 
scale comparable to a larger adviser with significantly more RAUM.

meaningful measure of adviser size for RFA purposes, because those 
metrics do not directly relate to how an adviser would scale resources

provide as meaningful a measure of adviser size for RFA purposes as an 
RAUM-based threshold. Advisers have diverse fee structures, and as a 
result, annual receipts may not correlate with firm scale, operational 
complexity, or available compliance resources. A commenter agreed,

b. The $1 Billion RAUM Threshold

$1 billion. Commenters generally agreed that the current RAUM Threshold 
is too low.\94\ Most commenters supported raising the RAUM Threshold to 
correct the misalignment between the current threshold and the current 
economic reality created by decades of industry growth,\95\ the fact

industry since the 1998 amendments, including that in 2010, the Dodd-
Frank Act raised the SEC-registration threshold, resulting in fewer 
smaller advisers registering with the Commission.\97\ In contrast, one 
commenter asserted it is counterintuitive that advisers' significantly 
increased RAUM supports their designation as small entities.\98\ 
Another commenter stated that the Commission should not base the RAUM 
Threshold on the fact that there are some very large advisers.\99\

    After considering comments, and in light of the RFA's default 
definitions and our data analysis, we continue to believe that a $1 
billion RAUM Threshold is appropriate, and we do not believe that the 
final rules would inappropriately afford larger firms RFA 
accommodations that are intended for small entities.\124\ A size 
standard threshold that is set too high could inadvertently cause 
Commission RFA analysis to mistakenly focus on issues of more general 
concern to the industry, instead of on issues that particularly impact 
smaller entities, as required by the RFA. Conversely, we are concerned 
that setting the RAUM Threshold too low would not be consistent with 
the RFA's default definition of ``small business'' and ``small 
organization,'' because it would exclude advisers that are not dominant 
in their field. We believe such advisers may have fewer compliance 
resources, and therefore, would benefit from being considered a ``small 
business'' or ``small organization'' under the RFA. Although using $1 
billion as the RAUM Threshold would classify a large proportion of 
investment advisers as small, this is a reasonable and appropriate 
result for purposes of our analyses under the RFA, in part due to the 
relative amount of

[[Page 69965]]

assets managed by these advisers compared to the largest advisers, 
i.e., those dominant in their field. We continue to believe that a $1 
billion RAUM Threshold strikes an appropriate balance between the level 
of RAUM per small adviser and the proportion of total RAUM in the 
industry captured by the new threshold.\125\

An ``exempt reporting adviser'' is an investment adviser that qualifies

Advisers Act to not assess the burden on exempt reporting advisers

businesses to different regulatory regimes. We are not persuaded to 
raise the RAUM Threshold higher for exempt reporting advisers than for 
SEC-registered advisers, because, in our experience, we do not believe 
exempt reporting advisers and SEC-registered advisers would be subject

could have similar business models or operational structures that could 
allow them to achieve similar economies of scale to implement certain

    The current rule provides that an adviser is a small entity if it 
has assets under management of less than $25 million ``or such higher 
amount as the Commission may by rule deem appropriate under Section 
203A(a)(1)(A) of the Act.'' Advisers Act section 203A(a)(1)(A) 
prohibits advisers from registering with the SEC if they have assets 
under management below a certain amount. The Commission originally 
adopted the phrase in 1998 so the RAUM Threshold could increase in 
tandem with any increase in the minimum threshold for SEC 
registration.\129\ That has not happened in practice, however, despite 
the SEC registration threshold increasing in 2010.\130\ Accordingly, we 
proposed to remove ``or such higher amount as the Commission may by 
rule deem appropriate under Section 203A(a)(1)(A) of the Act (15 U.S.C. 
80b-3a(a)(1)(A)),'' because the revised RAUM Threshold would exceed and 
thus not align with the minimum threshold for adviser registration. The 
Commission did not receive any comments on this proposed change and is 
removing the phrase, as proposed.

2. The Total Assets Threshold
    The final amendments eliminate the Total Assets Threshold, which 
currently excludes from the definition of small entity any adviser that 
has total assets of $5 million or more.\131\ The Commission requested 
comment on whether to adjust or eliminate the Total Assets Threshold 
and proposed to amend the Total Assets Threshold to include an 
Inflation Adjustment Mechanism.\132\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

CFR 275.0-7(a)(2), which sets forth the Total Assets Threshold. The 
Commission is redesignating the Control Relationship Threshold from 
17 CFR 275.0-7(a)(3) to 17 CFR 275.0-7(a)(2) and making conforming 
amendments to remove references to total assets. The Commission also 
is removing 17 CFR 275.0-7(b)(2), which defines ``total assets,'' 
and redesignating the subparagraphs of 17 CFR 275.0-7(b), to account 
for that removal.

    The Total Assets Threshold was designed to enable the Commission to 
differentiate between small advisers and non-small advisers that may 
not have significant RAUM but do have significant assets related to a 
non-advisory line or component of their business.\133\ The Total Assets 
Threshold also worked in concert with the Control Relationship 
Threshold in capturing common types of advisory industry 
affiliations.\134\ The Commission had stated that an adviser in a 
control relationship with a large broker-dealer or other large 
financial services firm typically benefits from the financial and 
technical resources of the large firm, and that the large firm may 
handle much of the administrative and compliance needs of its 
affiliated adviser using resources not reflected in the adviser's 
client assets or business assets.\135\

devote incremental resources to comply with the rules affecting an

    After considering comments, we are eliminating the Total Assets 
Threshold. It is not necessary to maintain the Total Assets Threshold, 
because the RAUM Threshold and Control Relationship Threshold, as 
amended, are more reliable indicators of whether an adviser is a small 
entity for purposes of the RFA. Balance sheet assets, such as leases 
and equipment, do not reflect the scope of an advisory business as well 
as regulatory assets under management.\139\ Furthermore, we understand 
an adviser that has de minimis RAUM, but significant assets related to 
a non-advisory business may not be willing or able to allocate 
resources from the non-advisory line to an immaterial advisory business 
if the non-advisory line does not share comparable compliance 
requirements. For example, while advisers and broker-dealers may have 
some comparable compliance requirements under the Advisers Act and the 
Exchange Act, respectively, other compliance requirements are not 
easily scalable for both. For example, both advisers and broker-dealers 
must deliver 17 CFR 279.1, Part 3 and 17 CFR 249.641, respectively 
(``Form CRS'') to retail investors under the Advisers Act and the 
Exchange Act, respectively,\140\ but only advisers must file Form ADV 
Part 1A, as applicable.\141\ Therefore, a large broker-dealer under 
common control with an adviser with de minimis RAUM may be able to 
scale certain resources to the adviser concerning Form CRS, but not 
Form ADV Part 1A, because that requirement only concerns the adviser.

take into account the structure of business concerns and organizations

and ``small organization'' and to preclude entities with significant 
economic or financial resources from obtaining potential regulatory

continue to prevent affiliates of large advisers from obtaining 
potential regulatory benefits under the RFA. Currently and under the

has assets under management equal to or greater than the RAUM

3. The Control Relationship Threshold
    The Commission is amending the Control Relationship Threshold, with 
modifications from the proposal. Currently, the Control Relationship 
Threshold disqualifies an adviser from being considered small if it is 
in a control relationship with an affiliated adviser exceeding an 
assets under management test that mirrors the current RAUM Threshold of 
$25 million.\150\ To continue to maintain a consistent threshold 
between the Control Relationship Threshold and the RAUM Threshold, the 
Commission is amending the value of the Control Relationship Threshold 
to conform it to the revised $1 billion RAUM Threshold, including its 
corresponding Inflation Adjustment Mechanism, as proposed.\151\ Also, 
as proposed, the Commission is removing ``(or such higher amount as the 
Commission may deem appropriate)'' to further conform the Control 
Relationship Threshold with the revised RAUM Threshold, for which the 
Commission removed a similar phrase.\152\ In a change from the 
proposal, the Commission is removing from the Control Relationship 
Threshold the elements that concern the Total Assets Threshold, namely 
that an

[[Page 69967]]

adviser is disqualified from being considered a small entity if it has 
a control relationship with any person (other than a natural person) 
that had total assets of $5 million or more on the last day of the most 
recent fiscal year (as well as the proposed inflation adjustment to 
this amount).\153\ As discussed above, an RAUM threshold is a more 
reliable indicator of whether an adviser is a small entity than a total 
assets threshold.\154\ In another change from the proposal, the 
Commission is further amending the Control Relationship Threshold, 
after considering comments, to help advisers understand how to 
calculate the assets under management referenced in the Control 
Relationship Threshold, as discussed more fully below.\155\ As a 
result, under the final amendments, an adviser would meet the Control 
Relationship Threshold if it does not control, is not controlled by, 
and is not under common control with another investment adviser that 
has assets under management equal to or greater than the RAUM 
Threshold.

    A commenter recommended the Commission amend the Control 
Relationship Threshold to provide a special rule for insurance 
companies, so that an insurance company's affiliated institutional 
advisers would not be cumulated with an insurance company's affiliated 
retail advisers.\164\ This commenter stated that institutional advisers 
and retail advisers involve substantially different infrastructures, 
systems, and regulatory requirements, they do not share management or 
advisory personnel, they have distinct costs and burdens, and there are 
few opportunities for economies of scale between them. The commenter 
expressed concern that a retail adviser may be disproportionately and 
unfairly impacted by changes in Commission regulation if its assets 
under management are cumulated with an institutional adviser merely due

    We are not persuaded to provide a special rule for insurance 
companies, so that an insurance company's affiliated institutional 
advisers would not be cumulated with an insurance company's affiliated 
retail advisers. Currently, the requirements in rule 0-7 do not 
distinguish between retail advisers and institutional advisers. We are 
not persuaded that advisers should be treated differently under rule 0-
7 solely based on the fact that they are affiliated with an insurance 
company. We disagree with this commenter's assertion that an adviser's 
retail and institutional advisory businesses involve substantially 
different regulatory requirements. Retail and institutional advisory 
businesses involve substantially similar regulatory requirements, 
because both are subject to the Advisers Act, and the rules thereunder, 
among other things which do not generally differentiate between the 
type of client. Even if affiliated advisers choose different 
infrastructures, systems, management, or advisory personnel, there 
remain opportunities for economies of scale concerning compliance with 
and operation under the Advisers Act and the rules thereunder, even if 
some particular provisions do not apply to each adviser. Therefore, we 
disagree with the commenter's assertion that a retail adviser would be 
disproportionately or unfairly impacted by changes in Commission 
regulation if its assets under management are cumulated with an 
institutional adviser due to common control.
4. Conforming Amendments to Form ADV and the Adviser Hardship Exemption 
Rule
    The Commission is making conforming amendments to Form ADV, General 
Instruction 17, and Item 12 of Part 1A, as well as Advisers Act rule 
203-3(b), with modifications from the proposal. Form ADV is the uniform 
application for investment adviser registration and report form by 
exempt reporting advisers. General Instruction 17 summarizes the 
conditions for certain small advisers to apply for an

[[Page 69968]]

exemption from filing Form ADV electronically with the IARD. Item 12 of 
Part 1A requires an eligible SEC-registered adviser to report how it 
qualifies as a ``small business'' or ``small organization'' under rule 
0-7. It is designed to provide information to the public and the 
Commission about advisers, including information that enables the 
Commission to consider the effect of its regulations on small entities, 
as required by the RFA.\165\ Rule 203-3(b) sets forth conditions for 
certain small SEC-registered advisers to apply for a continuing 
hardship exemption from the requirement to make Advisers Act filings 
electronically with the IARD, among other things.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \165\ See Form ADV, Item 12 of Part 1A.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    As proposed, the Commission is making conforming amendments to Form 
ADV, including General Instruction 17 and Item 12, as well as rule 203-
3(b) to reflect the final amendments to the RAUM Threshold, the Control 
Relationship Threshold, and their corresponding inflation adjustments. 
Currently, General Instruction 17 states, in part, that an adviser is a 
small business, and may be eligible for a continuing hardship 
exemption, if it is required to answer Item 12 of Part 1A ``(because 
you have assets under management of less than $25 million)'' and it is 
able to respond ``no'' to each question in Item 12. As proposed, the 
Commission is removing the parenthetical ``(because you have assets 
under management of less than $25 million).'' This parenthetical is 
implicit, given that the sentence also directs advisers to Item 12, 
which provides the relevant instructions. Removing this phrase will 
avoid requiring the Commission to update it periodically, as the 
Commission adjusts the RAUM Threshold for inflation. Also, as proposed, 
the Commission is revising General Instruction 17 and rule 203-3(b) so 
they explicitly apply to an adviser that is either a ``small business'' 
or ``small organization,'' as Item 12 does, rather than just a ``small 
business.''
    In a change from the proposal, the Commission is making additional 
conforming amendments to Form ADV, Item 12 of Part 1A to remove 
references to the Total Assets Threshold, to reflect that the 
Commission is eliminating the Total Assets Threshold from rule 0-7. In 
connection with this change, the Commission also is amending rule 203-
3(b)(5) to remove the phrase ``that you were required to answer'' 
because it is no longer relevant in light of the amendments to Item 12. 
In another change from the proposal, the Commission is revising the 
language of Form ADV Item 12, so that it refers to rule 0-7, rather 
than re-stating the threshold, as proposed. This amendment does not 
change the substance of Item 12 as compared to the proposal. The 
purpose of this amendment is to help ensure Item 12 remains operative, 
without additional rulemaking, in light of future Commission orders 
that may adjust rule 0-7's threshold for inflation.
    One commenter supported the proposed amendments to Form ADV, 
discussing that the proposed amendments would help ensure internal 
consistency across Commission rules.\166\ This commenter, along with 
another commenter, recommended not imposing any additional reporting 
requirements.\167\ The Commission did not propose additional reporting 
requirements, and is not adopting additional reporting requirements at 
this time. A commenter requested the Commission quantify and analyze 
regulatory relief consequences, which the commenter described as 
Commission reporting, compliance, or procedural accommodations that 
would become newly available once firms qualify as small entities.\168\ 
We are confirming that rule 203-3(b) provides such an accommodation and 
its continuing hardship accommodation will become newly available once 
firms qualify as small entities.\169\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \166\ IAA Comment Letter.
    \167\ IAA Comment Letter; Proskauer Comment Letter.
    \168\ See Scarborough Comment Letter.
    \169\ Currently, the Commission's definition of ``small entity'' 
under the RFA is incorporated into the Commission's other rules and 
regulations only in connection with an adviser's responses to Form 
ADV (and this release is implementing corresponding amendments to 
the form) and rule 203-3(b). See infra footnote 189, and 
accompanying text.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

C. Periodic Future Adjustments

    The final amendments to rules 0-10 and 0-7 will, as proposed, 
provide an Inflation Adjustment Mechanism for periodic future 
adjustments of the asset-based thresholds used in these rules' small 
entity definitions.\170\ Specifically, the amendments provide that the 
Commission will issue an order every ten years adjusting: (i) the net 
asset threshold in the investment company small entity definition; and 
(ii) in the investment adviser small entity definition, the RAUM 
Threshold (which will also now have the effect of adjusting the Control 
Relationship Threshold). As proposed, the final amendments to rule 0-10 
and rule 0-7 will require that the adjustment of the asset-based 
thresholds be calculated by reference to the Personal Consumption 
Expenditures Chain-Type Price Index (the ``PCE Index'').\171\ The final 
amendments providing the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism will require 
rounding the investment company small entity net asset threshold to the 
nearest multiple of $1,000,000,000 and rounding the investment adviser 
small entity RAUM Threshold (and thus the Control Relationship 
Threshold) to the nearest multiple of $100,000,000.\172\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \170\ Final 17 CFR 270.0-10(c); final 17 CFR 275.0-7(c).
    \171\ See id.
    \172\ Final 17 CFR 275.0-7(c)(2) and final 17 CFR 270.0-
10(c)(2). Final 17 CFR 270.0-10 will require the net asset threshold 
for small entities be adjusted for inflation by dividing the year-
end value of the PCE Index for the calendar year preceding the 
calendar year in which the order is being issued, by the year-end 
value of the PCE Index for the calendar year in which any final rule 
that is adopted becomes effective, multiplying $10 billion (i.e., 
the final amendments' net asset threshold) by that quotient, and 
rounding the product to the nearest multiple of $1 billion. Final 17 
CFR 275.0-7(c)(2) will adjust the RAUM Threshold (and thus the 
Control Relationship Threshold) by starting with the same quotient 
but will multiply that by $1 billion, rounded to the nearest 
multiple of $100 million.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In order to adjust the asset-based thresholds for the ``small 
entity'' definitions as discussed above, the Commission considered an 
analysis of the distribution of fund and adviser assets and the growth 
in these assets over time. As described in the Proposing Release, 
however, these amended thresholds may become less useful over time due 
to growth in markets and any subsequent changes in the fund and adviser 
industries. The proposed Inflation Adjustment Mechanism was designed to 
ensure that the thresholds are adjusted every ten years, because the 
adjustment would be required by rule and effected through a Commission 
order.
    Some commenters supported the proposed inflation adjustments.\173\ 
Other commenters supported the goal of periodic adjustments, but 
expressed concern about the details of the proposal.\174\ For example, 
some commenters recommended the Commission use a shorter cadence for 
adjustments, such as five or seven years, to ensure that the thresholds 
remain reasonable.\175\ Some commenters recommended using an adjustment 
mechanism they consider more relevant than inflation, such as a broad-
based index of asset prices,\176\ or the proposal's own asset-based 
distribution

[[Page 69969]]

analysis for RAUM and net asset percentiles.\177\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \173\ See, e.g., NVCA Comment Letter.
    \174\ See, e.g., Federated Hermes Comment Letter.
    \175\ See, e.g., Sharma Comment Letter (recommending a five-year 
cadence); Federated Hermes Comment Letter and ICI Comment Letter 
(each recommending a seven-year cadence).
    \176\ Proskauer Comment Letter.
    \177\ See, e.g., Proskauer Comment Letter; ICI Comment Letter.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    After considering comments, we are adopting the Inflation 
Adjustment Mechanism substantially as proposed.\178\ Adjustments that 
the Commission makes mechanically by order could help maintain the 
thresholds at levels that reflect the buying power of money over time, 
without the need for Commission action through rulemaking.\179\ We 
expect, as discussed in the Proposing Release and by commenters, that 
the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism will prevent the thresholds in the 
small entity definitions from becoming less meaningful over time on 
account of anticipated changes in dollar value.\180\ Specifically, 
because a fund's or adviser's size is related to its ability to bear 
compliance costs, adjusting the asset-based thresholds is designed to 
account for potential increases in those compliance costs.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \178\ As discussed above, for advisers, we are removing the 
Total Assets Threshold and its corresponding inflation adjustment, 
and we are revising the Control Relationship Threshold to refer to 
the RAUM Threshold and its inflation adjustment in establishing the 
threshold under which an affiliated adviser may affect an adviser's 
small entity status. See sections II.B.2 and II.B.3.
    \179\ The Commission has historically incorporated periodic and 
mechanical adjustments to certain dollar-based thresholds in 
regulations affecting funds and investment advisers. These 
adjustments reflect that some level of change in dollar value is 
reasonably anticipated to occur in the future and help ensure that 
the rules' intended application remains consistent and relevant over 
time. See, e.g., 17 CFR 270.3c-7; 17 CFR 275.205-3; see also 
Proposing Release, at n.128 (discussing Commission releases that 
have used the PCE Index for inflation adjustment).
    \180\ See Proposing Release at section II.C; see also, e.g., CAI 
Comment Letter; IAA Comment Letter.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    While certain comments recommended a shorter adjustment cadence, 
the final amendments' Inflation Adjustment Mechanism reflects the same 
ten-year cadence as proposed. Given the distributions of different-
sized entities for funds and investment advisers, inflationary changes 
over shorter periods would generally not result in a meaningfully 
different set of funds and investment advisers being considered small 
entities under their respective definitions.\181\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \181\ See, e.g., supra footnotes 42-43 and 52 and accompanying 
text; supra footnotes 108-110 and accompanying text.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Likewise, after considering comments recommending an adjustment 
mechanism based on a metric other than inflation, we are adopting this 
aspect of the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism as proposed. We 
acknowledge that inflation may not perfectly represent growth in the 
fund and adviser industries. Nevertheless, as discussed above, our view 
continues to be that inflation adjustment is the most appropriate 
mechanism for periodically and mechanically adjusting the asset 
thresholds and implementing the adjustments by order. Inflation, unlike 
the asset-based distribution analysis mechanisms described by 
commenters, is a known factor for which a precise value can reliably be 
derived from a defined index. Periodically adjusting the thresholds to 
a set percentile from a distribution analysis would similarly be 
inappropriate. The percentile that resulted from the distribution 
analysis performed in the Proposing Release is particular to that data 
and set of facts and, therefore, is not necessarily indicative of the 
proportion of funds or advisers that should be deemed small entities in 
the future. In addition, performing the same or similar analysis to 
determine a future percentile based on then-current data would involve 
a level of analysis that would require a future rulemaking rather than 
an adjustment by Commission order. Similarly, we do not consider using 
a broad-based index of asset prices as the basis for adjustment as 
suggested by commenters to be appropriate in light of the breadth of 
fund and adviser strategies. Any one particular index of asset prices 
would not be appropriate for certain strategies, and if multiple 
indexes were used, this could result in different levels of adjustment 
depending on the index, as well as operational complexity.
    It is possible, but less predictable, that the asset-based 
thresholds may become less useful over time even taking the Inflation 
Adjustment Mechanism we are adopting into account (for example, with 
the advent of market events, changes in the makeup or distribution of 
size of the fund or adviser markets, or other industry changes). In 
this case, the Commission could consider performing appropriate 
analyses to propose amendments to the thresholds again in the future 
independent of the Inflation Adjustment Mechanism. Similarly, in the 
future, the Commission also could consider proposing a periodic 
adjustment approach using analysis other than one based on the 
Inflation Adjustment Mechanism.

D. Effective Date and Compliance Date

    The effective dates and compliance dates are as follows:
     Final amendments to rule 0-10 and rule 0-7 are effective 
February 4, 2027, which is 90 days from the date of publication in the 
Federal Register.
     Final amendments to rule 203-3 and Form ADV are effective, 
and have a compliance date of, February 4, 2027, which is 90 days from 
the date of publication in the Federal Register.
    One commenter recommended an implementation period of 180 days, so 
advisers can reassess their ``small entity'' status, update internal 
Form ADV filing procedures, train compliance and personnel on the 
revised Form ADV Item 12 logic and hardship exemption eligibility, and 
coordinate updates with third-party compliance vendors or filing 
service providers where applicable.\182\ We are not persuaded to 
provide an implementation period of 180 days. While additional SEC-
registered advisers will have to update their small entity status in 
Item 12 of Form ADV and will be newly eligible for the hardship 
exemption under rule 203-3(b), the information required to comply with 
the final amendments is readily available to advisers and the 
additional cost of the final amendments would be minimal. Also, as a 
practical matter, most advisers will have additional time to update 
their Form ADV because Form ADV does not require advisers to file an 
other-than-annual amendment to update Item 12; most advisers will 
update Item 12 as part of their regularly scheduled annual 
amendments.\183\ The compliance period for rule 203-3 and Form ADV is 
designed to provide the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority

AGENCY: Securities and Exchange Commission.

ACTION: Publication of list of rules scheduled for review.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Securities and Exchange Commission (``Commission'') is 
publishing a list of rules to be reviewed pursuant to section 610 of 
the Regulatory Flexibility Act. The list is published to provide the 
public with notice that these rules are scheduled for review by the 
agency and to invite public comment on whether the rules should be 
continued without change, or should be amended or rescinded to minimize 
any significant economic impact of the rules upon a substantial number 
of small entities.

DATES: This release was published in the Federal Register on October 
23, 2026. Comments should be submitted by November 23, 2026.

[[Page 66796]]


ADDRESSES: Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:

Electronic Comments

     Use the Commission's internet comment form (https://www.sec.gov/comments/s7-2026-37/list-rules-be-reviewed-pursuant-regulatory-flexibility-act); or
     Send an email to [email protected]. Please include 
File Number S7-2026-37 on the subject line.

Paper Comments

     Send paper comments to Vanessa A. Countryman, Secretary, 
U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, 
DC 20549-1090.

All submissions should refer to File Number S7-2026-37. This file 
number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help 
the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, 
please use only one method of submission. The Commission will post all 
comments on the Commission's website (https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/public-comments/s7-2026-37). Do not include personally 
identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only 
information that you wish to make available publicly. The Commission 
may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted 
material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Sandra Sojka, General Attorney, Office 
of the General Counsel, 202-551-4928.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The Regulatory Flexibility Act (``RFA''), 
codified at 5 U.S.C. 601 through 612, requires an agency to review its 
rules that have a significant economic impact upon a substantial number 
of small entities within 10 years of the publication of such rules as 
final rules. 5 U.S.C. 610(a). The purpose of the review is ``to 
determine whether such rules should be continued without change, or 
should be amended or rescinded . . . to minimize any significant 
economic impact of the rules upon a substantial number of such small 
entities.'' 5 U.S.C. 610(a). The RFA sets forth specific considerations 
that must be addressed in the review of each rule:
     The continued need for the rule;
     The nature of complaints or comments received concerning 
the rule from the public;
     The complexity of the rule;
     The extent to which the rule overlaps, duplicates or 
conflicts with other Federal rules, and, to the extent feasible, with 
state and local governmental rules; and
     The length of time since the rule has been evaluated or 
the degree to which technology, economic conditions, or other factors 
have changed in the area affected by the rule. 5 U.S.C. 610(b).
    The list below includes rules adopted in 2017 that may have a 
significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities 
(but excludes rules that have been substantially changed since 
adoption, rules that are minor amendments to previously adopted rules, 
and rules that are ministerial, procedural, or technical in nature). 
Where the Commission has previously made a determination of a rule's 
impact on small businesses, the determination is noted on the list.
    The Commission particularly solicits public comment on whether the 
rules in the release listed below affect small businesses in new or 
different ways than when first adopted. The release listed below is 
scheduled for review by staff of the Commission.

AGENCY: Securities and Exchange Commission.

ACTION: Proposed rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Securities and Exchange Commission (the ``Commission'') is 
proposing to amend the rule under the Investment Company Act of 1940 
(the ``Investment Company Act'') that permits securities transactions 
between a registered investment company and certain affiliates 
(referred to as ``cross trades''), subject to conditions. The proposed 
amendments are designed to expand the scope of securities that are 
eligible for cross trading, modernize the rule's conditions, and 
enhance investor protection. The Commission also proposes to require 
aggregated reporting of trading activity and cross trades in Form N-
PORT and Form N-MFP.

DATES: This proposal was published in the Federal Register on October 
15, 2026. Comments should be received on or before December 14, 2026.

ADDRESSES: Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:

Electronic Comments

File Number S7-2026-36 on the subject line.

Paper Comments

     Send paper comments to Vanessa A. Countryman, Secretary, 
Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 
20549-1090.

All submissions should refer to File Number S7-2026-36. This file 
number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help 
the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, 
please use only one method of submission. The Commission will post all 
comments on the Commission's website (https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/public-comments/s7-2026-36). Do not include personally 
identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only 
information that you wish to make publicly available. We may redact in 
part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is 
obscene or subject to copyright protection.
    Studies, memoranda, or other substantive items may be added by the 
Commission or staff to the comment file during this rulemaking. A

will be made available on the Commission's website. To ensure direct

    A summary of the proposal of not more than 100 words is posted on

Mokodean, Senior Special Counsel; or Brian M. Johnson, Assistant 
Director at (202) 551-6792, Investment Company Regulation Office,

(referenced in 17 CFR 274.150), and Form N-MFP (referenced in 17 CFR
