I. Introduction

A. Overview

    Section 17 of the Investment Company Act prohibits certain 
transactions with a registered investment company (a ``registered 
fund'') by its ``affiliated persons'' and their ``affiliated persons.'' 
\1\ Under

[[Page 65623]]

section 17(a), an affiliated person of a registered fund, or an 
affiliated person of such a person, is generally prohibited from 
knowingly selling any security or other property to, or purchasing any 
security or other property from, the registered fund when acting as a 
principal. This prohibition protects registered funds and their 
investors against overreaching or self-dealing by the registered fund's 
adviser, directors, and other affiliated persons by prohibiting 
affiliated transactions where one of the parties has both the ability 
and the pecuniary incentive to influence the actions of the investment 
company.\2\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ See 15 U.S.C. 80a-17. Under section 2(a)(3) of the 
Investment Company Act, an ``affiliated person'' of a registered 
fund is generally defined to include: (1) directors, officers, 
employees, and the investment adviser; (2) any person owning 5% or 
more of the registered fund's voting securities; (3) any person in 
which the registered fund owns 5% or more of the voting securities; 
and (4) any person directly or indirectly controlling, controlled 
by, or under common control with the registered fund. See 15 U.S.C. 
80a-2(a)(3).
    \2\ See, e.g., Investment Trusts and Investment Companies: 
Hearings on S. 3580 Before a Subcomm. of the Senate Comm. on Banking 
and Currency, 76th Cong., 3d Sess., at 256-59 (1940).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    These provisions, among other things, prohibit cross trades, that 
is, where a registered fund sells a portfolio investment to, or 
purchases a portfolio investment from, another fund or other person 
that is an affiliated person of the registered fund (or an affiliated 
person of such affiliated person).
    In cases where there is no overreach, however, cross trades may 
benefit registered funds in several ways. For example, cross trades 
allow affiliated registered funds to avoid some of the costs associated 
with open market trades, such as brokerage commissions, bid-ask 
spreads, and other transaction expenses, when buying and selling 
securities with affiliated parties. Thus, section 17(b) of the 
Investment Company Act provides that the Commission shall issue 
exemptive orders to permit principal transactions with affiliates, 
including cross trades, when evidence establishes that certain criteria 
are satisfied. These criteria are:
    (1) The terms of the transaction, including the consideration paid 
and received, are reasonable and fair and do not involve overreaching;
    (2) The transaction is consistent with each concerned registered 
fund's disclosed policies; and
    (3) The transaction is consistent with the general purposes of the 
Investment Company Act.\3\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \3\ See 15 U.S.C. 80a-17(b).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    To eliminate the need to file and process exemptive applications in 
situations where it appears likely that these statutory protections 
would be satisfied, the Commission adopted rule 17a-7 to permit cross 
trades of certain securities, subject to protective conditions that are 
based upon the requirements of section 17(b).\4\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \4\ See Exemption of Certain Purchase or Sale Transactions 
Between Affiliated Registered Investment Companies, Investment 
Company Act Release No. 4697 (Sept. 8, 1966) [31 FR 12092 (Sept. 16, 
1966)] (``1966 Adopting Release'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Rule 17a-7 allows cross trades between a registered fund and 
certain of its affiliates (including affiliated registered funds and 
others who share a common investment adviser) (``eligible 
affiliates''), subject to the following conditions: \5\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \5\ Eligible affiliates include an affiliated person of the 
registered fund, or an affiliated person of an affiliated person of 
the fund, that is: (1) another registered fund (including separate 
series); (2) another series of the same registered fund; or (3) 
another person whose affiliation is solely by reason of having a 
common investment adviser (or affiliated investment advisers), 
common directors, and/or common officers.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     The security that is cross traded has readily available 
market quotations;
     There is no brokerage commission, fee (except customary 
transfer fees), or other remuneration paid in connection with the cross 
trade, and no consideration involved other than cash payment against 
prompt delivery of the security; and
     The cross trade is consistent with the policy of each 
registered fund participating in the trade.
    Further, the rule places certain responsibilities upon a registered 
fund's board of directors (a ``board'') to adopt cross-trading 
procedures, oversee the registered fund's cross trades, and monitor 
potential conflicts. Specifically, the registered fund's board 
(including a majority of directors who are not interested persons of 
the registered fund) must adopt procedures reasonably designed to 
ensure that cross trades comply with rule 17a-7 and must approve 
changes to those procedures as the board deems necessary. The 
registered fund's board must also determine, no less frequently than 
quarterly, that all cross trades made during the preceding quarter 
complied with the procedures. The rule also requires the board to 
satisfy certain registered fund governance standards.\6\ Additionally, 
each participating registered fund must maintain certain records 
relating to its cross-trading procedures and transactions.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \6\ See 17 CFR 270.0-1(a)(7).

    Separate from section 17(a) of the Investment Company Act, cross 
trading also involves considerations under the Investment Advisers Act 
of 1940 (the ``Advisers Act''). Investment advisers have fiduciary 
duties to their clients, including registered funds, under the Advisers 
Act to serve the best interests of their clients and to seek best 
execution of a client's transactions.\7\ In addition, section 206(3) of 
the Advisers Act prohibits an investment adviser, directly or 
indirectly, from knowingly selling any security to or purchasing any 
security from a client without disclosing to the client the capacity in 
which the adviser is acting and obtaining the client's consent to the 
transaction.\8\ Rule 17a-7 currently does not provide exemptive relief 
from any provisions of the Advisers Act, and the proposed amendments 
likewise would not provide exemptive relief from these provisions. 
Compliance with rule 17a-7 also does not relieve a party engaging in a 
cross trade involving an Employee Retirement Income Security Act 
(``ERISA'') plan from complying with applicable ERISA provisions.

    Business development companies (``BDCs'') are also subject to 
restrictions on affiliated transactions under section 57 of the 
Investment Company Act. Section 57 differs in some respects from the 
provisions for registered funds under section 17.\9\ Pursuant to 
section 57(i) of the Investment Company Act, until the Commission 
adopts rules for BDCs under section 57, BDCs are permitted to rely on 
rule 17a-7 to the extent that rule 17a-7 would permit a cross trade 
that section 57 would otherwise restrict. This release primarily 
focuses on the restrictions of section 17 of the Investment Company Act 
and therefore refers to registered funds throughout, but BDCs may rely 
on rule 17a-7 unless the Commission adopts BDC-specific rules under 
section 57 of the Investment Company Act in the future. The discussion 
in this release applies equally to BDCs.

    \9\ For example, section 57 creates different categories of

B. Evolution of Funds' Cross-Trading Activities and Developments 
Underlying the Commission's Consideration of the Proposed Amendments

    In 1966, when the Commission first adopted rule 17a-7, trades in 
equity securities were subject to substantial brokerage charges. The 
rule served the interests of investors by permitting affiliated funds 
to transact with each other, and thus avoid the payment of these 
brokerage charges, in situations where the Commission was likely to 
grant an exemption under section 17(b).\10\ As a result, Rule 17a-7 
initially was limited to cross trades of equity securities that were 
traded on a national

[[Page 65624]]

securities exchange and for which objective pricing information was 
available on the exchange.\11\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \10\ See 1966 Adopting Release, supra note 4.
    \11\ The Commission later amended the rule to include securities 
transactions entered into on a national inter-dealer quotation 
system that met certain conditions. See Exemption for Securities 
Traded in Over-the-Counter Market and Change in Annual Report Form 
N-1R, Investment Company Act Release No. 8494 (Sept. 13, 1974) [39 
FR 36002 (Oct. 7, 1974)].
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In the early 1980s, recognizing that funds at that time 
increasingly invested in securities that traded over the counter but 
had an active trading market that generated independent pricing 
information, the Commission expanded the scope of rule 17a-7 to apply 
to trades involving any security for which market quotations are 
readily available.\12\ The Commission did not define the term ``readily 
available market quotations'' at that time. Because the rule was no 
longer limited to equity securities, over time, registered funds came 
to rely on rule 17a-7 to cross trade fixed-income securities as well.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \12\ See Exemption of Certain Purchase or Sale Transactions 
Between a Registered Investment Company and Certain Affiliated 
Persons Thereof, Investment Company Act Release No. 11676 (Mar. 10, 
1981) [46 FR 17011 (Mar. 17, 1981)] (``1981 Adopting Release'').
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    When expanding rule 17a-7 to permit cross trades of over-the-
counter securities, the Commission also amended the rule's pricing 
provisions to require that these trades be priced at the average of the 
highest current independent bid and lowest current independent offer 
determined on the basis of reasonable inquiry. Historically, to meet 
this ``reasonable inquiry'' standard, registered funds obtained 
multiple bids and offers from broker-dealers for an over-the-counter 
security. In 1981, when the reasonable inquiry standard was adopted, 
quotes for fixed-income securities were generally obtained by calling 
individual broker-dealers on the phone.
    Since that time, markets have undergone significant technological 
and structural changes, leading to pricing that is more verifiable, 
accessible, and transparent. For instance, fixed-income markets have 
seen developments in transparency, with Trade Reporting and Compliance 
Engine (TRACE) and Real-Time Transaction Reporting System (RTRS) 
reporting for many segments of the markets.\13\ In addition, there have 
been improvements in price discovery with the rise of electronic 
trading platforms, which can provide enhanced pre- and post-trade 
transparency. This includes, for example, systems that electronically 
display continuous trading interest (or ``stream axes'') in a security 
or type of security on the system and ``request for quote'' (or 
``RFQ'') systems that are designed to allow market participants to 
obtain quotes for a particular security by sending messages to one or 
multiple potential respondents on the system simultaneously. Fixed-
income exchange-traded funds (``ETFs''), which trade throughout the day 
and reflect what the market believes to be the price of their 
underlying portfolios, also can serve as meaningful price discovery 
vehicles.\14\ Moreover, many registered funds engage third-party 
pricing services to provide pricing information.\15\ In the context of 
cross trading municipal securities, certain letters from the Division 
of Investment Management staff (``staff'') have addressed a fund's use 
in cross trades of the price provided by an independent pricing service 
that values the fund's municipal securities for purposes of determining 
the fund's net asset value (``NAV'').\16\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \13\ FINRA's TRACE (introduced in 2002) is an over-the-counter

    The evolution of the registered fund industry in part drove 
increased demand to cross trade fixed-income securities. In the last 
twenty years, registered funds that invest primarily in fixed-income 
instruments have expanded from around $1.5 trillion in assets to 
approximately $7.9 trillion.\17\ Further, according to an industry 
survey, registered funds engaged in more than $200 billion in cross 
trades of fixed-income securities in 2020 alone, resulting in estimated 
savings for those registered funds and their shareholders of over $300 
million.\18\

    In December 2020, the Commission adopted 17 CFR 270.2a-5 (``rule 
2a-5'') under the Investment Company Act, which addresses fund 
valuation practices and the board's role with respect to the fair value 
of a fund's investments.\19\ Among other things, rule 2a-5 defines the 
term ``readily available market quotations'' because the requirement to 
determine a security or other asset's fair value under the Investment 
Company Act and rule 2a-5 applies to securities and assets for which 
there are no readily available market quotations.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \19\ See Valuation Rule Adopting Release, supra note 15.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Rule 2a-5 provides that market quotations are readily available 
with respect to a security only when that ``quotation is a quoted price 
(unadjusted) in active markets for identical investments that the fund 
can access at the measurement date, provided that a quotation will not 
be readily available if it is not reliable.'' \20\ This definition is 
consistent with the definition of a level 1 input in the fair value 
hierarchy outlined in U.S. generally accepted accounting principles 
(``GAAP'').\21\ However, this definition practically excludes most 
fixed-income securities from meeting the readily available market 
quotation standard because fixed-income securities trade infrequently 
and thus usually do not have active markets that provide the direct 
observable pricing inputs necessary to meet the standard.\22\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \20\ See rule 2a-5(c); Valuation Rule Adopting Release, supra 
note 15.
    \21\ See Financial Accounting Standards Board Accounting 
Standards Codification (``ASC'') Topic 820-10-20. ASC Topic 820

priority to quoted, observable inputs (level 1) and the lowest 
priority to unobservable inputs (level 3).
    \22\ We understand that most fixed-income securities are not 
level 1 securities for U.S. GAAP purposes but rather are typically 
classified as level 2 securities.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

public as it considered potential revisions to the rule.

C. Current Cross Trading Considerations

    While markets have changed significantly since the Commission first 
adopted rule 17a-7 in 1966, response letters to the Staff Statement 
identify benefits that cross trades continue to offer to registered 
funds and their investors. For example, cross trading can help a 
registered fund avoid transaction costs that it would otherwise incur 
in open market transactions and counterparty risks.\35\ Cross trading 
also can help a registered fund avoid market impacts, including price 
movement and price uncertainty, if the registered fund seeks to 
increase or reduce a position that is large enough to move the price of 
that security, and can provide greater execution speed and certainty 
relative to open market transactions.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \35\ See, e.g., ICI Letter; Wellington Letter; SIFMA AMG Letter. 
For example, if a bond is trading on the open market with a bid of 
$100.00 and an ask of $100.50, then a selling fund would receive 
$100.00 for the bond in the open market, while a buying fund would 
pay $100.50 for the bond. If the funds instead cross traded the 
bond, they could transact at the midpoint price of $100.25 and each 
realize a benefit of $0.25.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Apart from potential benefits in transaction costs and pricing, 
cross trades can provide registered funds access to difficult to obtain 
securities that an advisory client might otherwise sell into the market 
due to redemption

[[Page 65626]]

activity or other portfolio management considerations. Cross trading 
also can provide an alternative source of liquidity for a selling 
registered fund where an affiliated fund or other account would benefit 
from purchasing the security in the cross trade, which can be an 
important benefit if few broker-dealers maintain an inventory of the 
security. Because of these benefits, it continues to be an appropriate 
use of our authority under sections 6(c) and 17(b) of the Investment 
Company Act to exempt cross-trading activity, subject to appropriate 
controls to prevent abuse or overreach.\36\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \36\ Under section 6(c) of the Investment Company Act, the 
Commission may by rule, regulation, or order exempt any person or 
transaction or any class of persons or transactions from any 
provision of the Act if and to the extent that such exemption is 
necessary or appropriate in the public interest and consistent with 
protection of investors and the purposes fairly intended by the 
policy and provisions of the Act. See 15 U.S.C. 80a-6(c).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    While cross trades can provide significant benefits, cross trades 
also can implicate conflicts of interest in that an adviser may have 
the incentive, and ability, to favor one client over another to achieve 
higher advisory fees or other benefits for the adviser. These conflicts 
can lead to a registered fund being disadvantaged by its adviser in 
favor of higher-fee paying clients or other accounts, particularly when 
a security or other instrument is thinly traded. Examples of possible 
cross-trading abuses include:
     ``Parking,'' where an adviser may pre-arrange a cross 
trade with the intent to purchase the securities back at prices that 
disadvantage clients and evade regulatory oversight.\37\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \37\ See, e.g., In the Matter of Morgan Stanley Investment 
Management Inc. and Sheila Huang, Investment Company Act Release No. 
31947 (Dec. 22, 2015) (settled enforcement action alleging that a 
portfolio manager prearranged trades between affiliates at prices 
that favored certain clients over others and effected such trades 
through a broker-dealer to evade the firm's internal cross-trade 
procedures); In the Matter of Western Asset Management Co., 
Investment Company Act Release No. 30893 (Jan. 27, 2014) (settled 
enforcement action alleging engagement in dealer-interposed cross 
trades at prices that favored one side over another).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     ``Cherry-picking,'' where more desirable investments are 
cross traded to a favored or more profitable client.\38\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \38\ See, e.g., In the Matter of SeaCrest Wealth Management, 
LLC, Advisers Act Release No. 6788 (Dec. 12, 2024) (settled 
enforcement action alleging that block trades were allocated among 
client accounts in a manner that favored some accounts over others).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     ``Dumping'' where less desirable investments are cross 
traded to a less favored client.\39\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \39\ See, e.g., In the Matter of Macquarie Investment Management 
Business Trust, Investment Company Act Release No. 35325 (Sept. 19, 
2024) (settled enforcement action alleging internal and dealer-
interposed cross trades that were executed at prices that deviated 
from current market prices, causing certain purchasing accounts 
(primarily registered funds) to absorb trading losses that otherwise 
would have been borne by the selling unregistered pooled investment 
vehicles).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    As a result, cross trading must be subject to appropriate 
conditions, and registered funds must have effective and robust 
oversight mechanisms to guard against these potential conflicts.
    Cross trading also has the potential to negatively affect price 
discovery and market integrity if large volumes of trades occur between 
affiliated parties. Unlike open market transactions, information about 
individual cross trades, such as the price, size, and instrument 
involved in the trade, generally is not publicly reported. The lack of 
transparency about the prices at which cross trades are effected may 
negatively affect the market's price discovery processes. Similarly, 
the lack of information about the volume of cross trades may distort 
perceptions of the liquidity of a particular asset class or market. The 
lack of cross-trade information may reduce the broader market's ability 
to accurately assess the value of certain securities or asset classes. 
As a result, some degree of transparency about funds' cross-trading 
activities is necessary.

D. Overview of Proposal

    We propose to modernize and expand rule 17a-7 to better allow cross 
trades that are beneficial to registered funds and their shareholders, 
while also updating the rule's conditions to ensure effective investor 
protection: \40\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \40\ The exemptions proposed would be necessary and appropriate 
in the public interest and consistent with the protection of 
investors and the purposes fairly intended by the policy and 
provisions of the Investment Company Act.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     Expand securities eligible to be cross traded. We propose 
to expand the types of securities eligible for trading under the rule 
to include securities that the registered fund values based on inputs 
that are observable, either directly or indirectly. This change would 
permit cross trading of most fixed-income securities under the proposed 
rule because observable inputs are available for most fixed-income 
securities. The proposed change would limit the universe of securities 
eligible for trading under the rule to securities that have an 
independent basis for pricing, including those with readily available 
market quotations and observable inputs, to reduce the risk of 
subjectivity, bias, or error in determining the price of the cross 
trade.
     Updated pricing conditions. Recognizing the current 
pricing conditions may not be well suited to modern markets, we propose 
to update the pricing conditions of the rule to require the cross trade 
be effected using one of two pricing methods, which would be considered 
the independent current market price for purposes of the rule. The 
first pricing method would use the value of the security determined in 
the registered fund's next computation of NAV. Under the second method, 
the cross trade would be effected at a price that the registered fund's 
investment adviser determines reasonably represents the current market 
price for the security using one or more unaffiliated pricing sources. 
If the registered fund uses the second method, the fund's investment 
adviser would be required to periodically review the reasonableness of 
these prices.
     Conflict oversight and recordkeeping. In lieu of the 
rule's current board oversight requirements, the proposal would make a 
number of changes to the current rule designed to enhance investor 
protection and allocate oversight responsibility in an effective 
manner. In the first instance, the registered fund's adviser would be 
required to determine prior to effecting a transaction that the 
proposed cross trade is in the best interest of the fund. Additionally, 
the registered fund's CCO would be required to perform quarterly 
reviews of cross trades to determine compliance with the rule and 
report the results to the fund's board. The CCO would also be required 
to conduct at least annual back testing of cross trades, which must 
include analyses of the ultimate prices realized when any security 
purchased by a fund through a cross trade is ultimately sold, to look 
for patterns suggesting disadvantages to the fund relative to 
affiliates and report the results to the board. Funds would be required 
to maintain and preserve records of each cross trade, the information 
and material used by the CCO to make the required determinations 
(including the information and material used to determine at least 
quarterly whether the conditions of the rule were satisfied for each 
cross trade and for the at least annual disposition-based and other 
back-testing to identify potential abuses), and reports provided to the 
board.
     Reporting. Registered funds do not currently report 
information about their cross trades in a structured way. Additional 
reporting about a fund's cross-trading activity in the context of its 
overall trading activity would help investors, the Commission, and 
other market participants better understand the scope and breadth of 
cross-trading activities and how these activities relate

[[Page 65627]]

to, and affect, other reported market information. The proposal would 
add requirements for registered funds that engage in cross-trading 
activities to report--on Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP--aggregate 
information, by asset class, about the value of securities a registered 
fund traded during the preceding month and corresponding information 
about cross-trading activity by asset class.
     Other modernizations. The proposed rule 17a-7 amendments 
would also expressly permit de minimis payments to unaffiliated parties 
for services such as clearing, settlement, and custody. In addition, 
the proposed amendments would provide that a cross trade must be 
consistent with the registered fund's policies and investment 
strategies. For clarity, we also propose to add defined terms to the 
rule related to the registered funds that may rely on the rule and the 
eligible affiliates with which they may cross trade. The proposed 
defined terms would not modify these aspects of the current rule.

II. Discussion

A. Eligible Securities Expansion

    We propose to amend rule 17a-7 to expand the scope of securities 
that are eligible to be cross traded under the rule. The proposed 
amendments would permit cross trading of securities that would be 
valued by a registered fund based on inputs that are observable, either 
directly or indirectly, in addition to those with readily available 
market quotations.\41\ By expanding the eligible securities for funds 
to cross trade to include those with observable inputs, the proposal is 
designed to expand the benefits of cross trading to more transactions 
while protecting investors by ensuring that there is an independent 
basis for determining the price of the security.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \41\ See proposed rule 17a-7(b)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Rule 17a-7 currently restricts the scope of securities that are 
eligible to be cross traded to securities for which market quotations 
are readily available.\42\ In 1981, when the Commission amended the 
rule to include this condition, the Commission stated that reliance on 
readily available market quotations provides an independent basis for 
determining that the terms of the transaction are fair and reasonable 
to each participating registered fund and do not involve 
overreaching.\43\ The Commission further stated that this condition 
would limit cross trading to securities that trade in active secondary 
markets, making the securities more likely to have independent pricing 
information available.\44\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \42\ See current rule 17a-7(a).
    \43\ See 1981 Adopting Release, supra note 12.
    \44\ Id.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Rule 2a-5 under the Investment Company Act, which the Commission 
adopted in 2020, defines readily available market quotations to mean 
that there is a quoted price (unadjusted) in active markets for 
identical investments that the fund can access at the measurement date, 
provided that a quotation will not be readily available if it is not 
reliable.\45\ This definition is consistent with the definition of a 
``level 1'' input in the fair value hierarchy outlined in U.S. 
GAAP.\46\ A security is considered to have readily available market 
quotations if its value is determined solely by reference to level 1 
inputs.\47\ Under the proposed rule 17a-7 amendments, funds would 
continue to be allowed to cross trade securities that have readily 
available market quotations as defined in rule 2a-5 (i.e., level 1 
securities).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \45\ See rule 2a-5(c).
    \46\ See Valuation Rule Adopting Release, supra note 15, at 
section II.D; ASC Topic 820-10-20.
    \47\ See id., at paragraph accompanying n.336.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    We understand that most fixed-income securities that registered 
funds seek to trade do not have readily available market quotations 
because, among other reasons, they are not frequently traded in the 
secondary market and therefore are not valued solely by reference to 
level 1 inputs. As discussed above, such securities generally have not 
been eligible to cross trade since the compliance date for rule 2a-
5.\48\ The Commission also understands that cross trading fixed-income 
securities could provide benefits to registered funds and registered 
fund shareholders, including, for example, lower transaction costs and 
access to difficult to obtain securities.\49\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \48\ See current rule 17a-7(a); supra note 23 and accompanying 
text.
    \49\ See, e.g., Lina Han et. al., Cross Trading in in the 
Corporate Bond Market, SMU Cox Sch. of Bus., Research Paper No. 25-
15 (2025) (stating that registered funds may benefit from cross 
trading due to, among other things, the funds avoiding transaction 
costs and obtaining difficult to obtain bonds); ICI Letter (stating 
that amending rule 17a-7 to permit registered funds to cross trade 
fixed-income securities, subject to certain conditions, would 
benefit funds and investors by lowering transaction costs).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    To recognize those benefits while still protecting investors, we 
propose to expand the scope of securities that are eligible to be cross 
traded under the rule to include securities that are valued by 
registered funds based on inputs that are observable, either directly 
or indirectly (``level 2 securities''). This proposed change--that a 
security valued based on direct or indirect observable inputs would be 
eligible--is designed to be consistent with the current definition of a 
level 2 input in the fair value hierarchy outlined in U.S. GAAP.\50\ 
Level 2 inputs include, for example, quoted prices for similar 
securities in active markets, quoted prices for identical or similar 
securities in non-active markets, and inputs other than quoted prices 
that are observable for the security, such as credit spreads or 
interest rates and yield curves that are observable at commonly quoted 
intervals.\51\ For purposes of the proposed rule, we would consider a 
security to be valued based on inputs that are observable, either 
directly or indirectly, only to the extent that level 2 inputs are the 
lowest level of inputs that are significant to the entire 
measurement.\52\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \50\ See ASC 820-10-20; ASC 820-10-35-47 (providing that level 2 
inputs are inputs other than quoted prices included within level 1 
that are observable for the asset or liability, either directly or 
indirectly). Observable inputs are those that are developed using 
market data, such as publicly available information about actual 
events or transactions, and that reflect the assumptions that market 
participants would use when pricing the security. See ASC 820-10-20 
(defining ``observable inputs'').
    \51\ See ASC 820-10-35-48.
    \52\ See ASC 820-10-35-37A (providing that where the inputs used 
to measure the fair value of an asset or liability are categorized 
within different levels of the fair value hierarchy, the fair value 
measurement is categorized in its entirety in the same level of the 
fair value hierarchy as the lowest level of input that is 
significant to the entire measurement).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Although level 2 securities do not have readily available market 
quotations like level 1 securities, they do have other observable 
inputs, such as quoted prices or prices for similar assets, that can be 
independently verified and often have multiple pricing sources 
available. Requiring observable pricing inputs for cross trading 
eligibility reduces the potential for overreaching of the registered 
fund by the adviser, and would increase the likelihood that the terms 
of a cross trade are fair and reasonable to each participating 
registered fund consistent with the provisions for exemptive relief 
under section 17(b) of the Investment Company Act. Therefore, we 
propose to expand the scope of securities that are eligible to be cross 
traded to include securities that would be valued by the registered 
fund based on inputs that are observable, either directly or 
indirectly, which we understand would include many fixed-income 
securities.\53\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \53\ According to an industry survey, 99.6% of the fixed-income 
securities that funds that responded to the survey cross traded in 
2020 were classified as level 2 securities. See ICI Letter.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Securities valued based on unobservable inputs that are significant

[[Page 65628]]

to the entire measurement (i.e., ``level 3'' inputs under U.S. GAAP) or 
that are non-leveled under U.S. GAAP (i.e., investments that are not 
categorized within the fair value hierarchy, certain private fund-
issued securities that are valued using those private fund shares' NAV 
as a practical expedient) would not be eligible for cross trading under 
the proposal.\54\ Given the conflicts of interest implicated by cross 
trades and the importance of the transaction price to ensure that a 
cross trade is fair and reasonable to each participating registered 
fund and does not involve overreaching, we propose to permit cross 
trading under rule 17a-7 only of securities corresponding to assets 
whose fair value measurement is categorized as level 1 or level 2 
within the current U.S. GAAP fair value hierarchy.\55\ The proposed 
approach is designed to focus on securities that have an independent 
basis for pricing, including those with readily available market 
quotations and observable inputs, thus reducing the risk of 
subjectivity, bias, or error in determining the price of the cross 
trade.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \54\ See, e.g., ASC 820-10-35-51 (``An adjustment to a Level 2 
input that is significant to the entire measurement might result in 
a fair value measurement categorized within Level 3 of the fair 
value hierarchy if the adjustment uses significant unobservable 
inputs''); ASC 820-10-15-4 through 15-5; ASC 820-10-35-59 through 
35-62 (permitting a security that does not have a readily 
determinable fair value to be valued based on the issuer's net asset 
value per share (or its equivalent) as a practical expedient under 
certain circumstances).
    \55\ Overall, registered funds' holdings of level 3 investments 
are small in comparison to level 1 and level 2 investments. For 
example, based on a review of Form N-PORT filings as of February 
2026, less than 1% of the total value of all reporting funds' 
investments were in level 3 investments. Of the investments that 
funds reported as level 3, it was more common for investments in the 
loan, equity preferred, and real estate asset classes to be reported 
as level 3 than investments in other asset classes.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    These proposed amendments are designed to allow cross trading of 
securities that have an independent basis for pricing the trade as they 
are less likely to raise the same concerns regarding overreaching that 
rule 17a-7 was designed to address. This, in combination with the 
proposal's other conditions, are designed to expand the benefits of 
cross trading to more funds and shareholders while protecting investors 
from the conflicts of interest implicated by cross trades.
    We request comment on the proposed eligible securities 
requirements.
    1. Instead of expanding the rule to include level 2 securities, 
should we further broaden or narrow the scope of securities that are 
eligible for cross trading? If so, which securities should be eligible 
for cross trading, why, and under what circumstances? Do those 
securities have an independent basis for valuation and low risk of 
subjectivity, bias, or error in determining the price of a cross trade, 
thus making it more likely that the terms of the cross trade would be 
fair and reasonable to each participating fund?
    2. If we allow funds to cross trade a broader scope of securities 
than proposed (e.g., all or certain types of level 3 securities), 
should we include other conditions beyond those that we propose? Should 
those conditions apply to cross trades of all permitted securities, or 
only to certain types of securities? How would those conditions address 
the potential for overreaching or conflicts of interest when securities 
may lack an independent, observable basis for valuation? For example, 
should we require prior trade-by-trade board or board committee 
approval, including by a majority of directors who are not interested 
persons of the fund, for cross trades of securities that are not level 
1 or level 2 securities, or additional pricing, documentation, 
escalation, and post-trade review processes to verify pricing fairness 
for cross trades of such securities (e.g., the cross-trade price must 
be aligned with the valuation determined for purposes of the fund's 
NAV, portfolio managers must obtain advance written approval from the 
fund's board or CCO to cross trade these securities, the fund must 
report details of these cross trades to the Commission or the public, 
or cross trades of these securities must be reviewed by the CCO and 
reported to the board more frequently than the quarterly reviews the 
proposal would require)?
    3. Are there any types of securities that registered funds 
currently cross trade under rule 17a-7 that would no longer be eligible 
to cross trade under the proposed amendments to rule 17a-7?
    4. Are there securities that would be included within the scope of 
the proposed eligibility conditions that commenters believe should not 
be eligible for cross trading? If so, which securities and why?
    5. The proposed approach tracks concepts in current U.S. GAAP 
related to valuation. Should we use these concepts for defining the 
scope of eligible securities that registered funds can cross trade? Are 
there potential unintended consequences that could arise from linking 
the rule to concepts in current U.S. GAAP? Should we use a different 
approach to define the scope of eligible securities and, if so, what 
approach should we use for this purpose? For example, should the scope 
of eligible securities be based on asset class?
    6. Rather than limit the scope of securities that registered funds 
can cross trade, should we permit funds to cross trade any security 
provided that other conditions of the rule are met? If funds should be 
permitted to cross trade any security, please explain why other 
conditions in the rule would be sufficient to address overreaching and 
conflicts of interest or whether there are additional conditions that 
should apply to such cross trades.

B. Pricing of Cross Trades

    We propose to amend rule 17a-7 to provide two alternative methods 
for pricing cross trades. Under the proposal, a cross trade would be 
effected at the independent current market price, which for purposes of 
rule 17a-7 would be either:
    (1) The value of the security determined in the registered fund's 
next net asset value computation on the business day of the cross trade 
(``NAV pricing''); or
    (2) A price that reasonably represents the current market price, as 
determined by the registered fund's adviser using one or more 
unaffiliated pricing sources (``current market pricing''), provided 
that the adviser periodically reviews the reasonableness of such 
prices.\56\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \56\ See proposed rule 17a-7(b)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The proposed pricing provisions are designed to recognize 
developments since the Commission last amended this aspect of the rule, 
including the availability of more verifiable, accessible, and 
transparent pricing information, and the adoption of rule 2a-5, which 
led to enhancements to the regulatory framework for fund valuations. 
The proposal is designed to help address conflicts of interest that 
could incentivize cross trading at a price that is more favorable to an 
eligible affiliate than to the registered fund.
    Rule 17a-7 currently prescribes different methods for determining 
the price of a cross trade, depending principally on whether the 
security is exchange listed or traded over the counter. For example, 
for most listed equity securities other than options, the price of the 
cross trade is the last sale price with respect to the security 
reported in the consolidated transaction reporting system or, if there 
are no reported transactions that day, the average of the highest 
current independent bid and lowest current independent offer for such 
security. For fixed-income securities and other securities traded over 
the counter, in contrast, the price of the cross trade is the average 
of the highest current independent bid and lowest current

[[Page 65629]]

independent offer determined on the basis of reasonable inquiry.\57\ As 
discussed above, prior to the adoption of rule 2a-5, registered funds 
cross traded some fixed-income securities. We understand that 
registered funds cross trading such securities generally satisfied the 
rule's pricing requirements by gathering multiple bids and offers from 
broker-dealers.\58\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \57\ See current rule 17a-7(b).
    \58\ See, e.g., United Municipal Bond Fund, SEC Staff No-Action 
Letter (July 30, 1992).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Several letters in response to the Staff Statement and other staff 
outreach addressed the rule's current pricing requirements, including 
feedback that the pricing provisions should be broader and more 
flexible. For example, some suggested that funds should be able to 
price cross trades using multiple inputs and sources of data, including 
independent evaluated prices and broker-dealer quotes.\59\ Some 
supported use of independent pricing sources providing evaluated prices 
that are used for valuation purposes under rule 2a-5.\60\ In light of 
this feedback, the improvements in transparency and price discovery 
methods available, as well as the significant diversity in how 
different types of investments are priced, the pricing requirements of 
the proposed rule are designed to provide funds with the ability to 
price a cross trade flexibly and efficiently while maintaining investor 
protections. We also recognize that price discovery methods are likely 
to continue to evolve, and the proposed approach is intended to be 
dynamic rather than identifying particular pricing sources that funds 
must or may use.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \59\ See, e.g., ICI Letter; IAA Letter; Letter of Capital Group 
(May 6, 2021) (``Capital Group Letter'').
    \60\ See, e.g., ICI Letter; Capital Group Letter; DFA Letter.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In addition to proposing to expand the scope of securities eligible 
for cross trading by registered funds beyond those with readily 
available market quotations (level 1 securities) to also include 
securities valued based on directly or indirectly observable inputs 
(level 2 securities), we propose that each cross trade would be 
effected at the independent current market price determined using one 
of two pricing methodologies, either NAV pricing or current market 
pricing. A registered fund may switch between the two pricing 
methodologies for different cross trades. Pricing under the proposal 
would be subject to controls and oversight. If a fund uses NAV pricing 
for cross trades, the price of a cross trade would be subject to 
existing valuation processes and oversight procedures compliant with 
rule 2a-5 designed to ensure those prices are reasonable. If a fund 
uses current market pricing for cross trades, it would need to develop 
processes and oversight procedures to support the determination that 
the price reasonably represents the current market price and to comply 
with the proposed requirement for the adviser to periodically review 
the reasonableness of these prices. This approach is intended to 
address concerns respondents raised about the existing pricing 
provisions while promoting reasonable and fair pricing of cross trades. 
These pricing-specific conditions are designed to work with other 
proposed controls and oversight to promote investor protection, such as 
the investment adviser's best interest determination.
1. NAV Pricing
    We propose to amend rule 17a-7 to provide that a cross trade could 
be effected at the price determined by using NAV pricing. The 
transaction would be effected at the value the registered fund ascribes 
to the security in its next computation of the registered fund's 
current net asset value under section 2(a)(41) of the Investment 
Company Act and 17 CFR 270.2a-4 (``rule 2a-4'') and rule 2a-5 on the 
business day on which the transaction occurs. By leveraging existing 
valuation processes that are already subject to robust controls and 
oversight, the NAV pricing approach is designed to be a cost-effective 
method of pricing cross trades that would limit the potential for 
abuses.
    Under this proposed approach, the cross-trade price would be 
determined by the registered fund's next computation of its NAV on the 
business day of the cross trade. Many registered funds make NAV 
determinations at the close of business each day, and some funds--such 
as some money market funds and ETFs--make NAV determinations intra-day. 
Under the proposal, the registered fund would use the value determined 
in the next NAV computation on that day, whether it is at close of 
business or intra-day. Registered funds, such as some closed-end funds, 
that do not compute their NAVs on a daily basis would be permitted to 
use the NAV pricing approach only on days that their NAVs are computed. 
If a cross trade involves two registered funds, the registered funds 
must share the same valuation processes so that they would arrive at 
the same price using the NAV pricing approach. For registered funds 
that have valuation processes, such as the pricing sources used, that 
could result in different valuation outcomes under the NAV pricing 
approach, the cross-trade price could only be determined under the 
current market pricing approach.
    The NAV pricing approach would establish a standard that is 
consistent with the registered fund's valuation policies and procedures 
and that would apply to all types of securities that funds may cross 
trade, while allowing for differences in how various types of 
securities are priced. Specifically, when using NAV pricing, the cross-
trade price would be either the current market value (in the case of 
securities with readily available market quotations) or the fair value 
(in the case of other securities and assets) based on observable inputs 
determined in the registered fund's next NAV computation.\61\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \61\ See section 2(a)(41) under the Investment Company Act; 17 
CFR 270.2a-4; 17 CFR 270.2a-5.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The proposed rule would not, however, permit use of the amortized 
cost value of a security that some money market funds are permitted to 
use for purposes of computing their NAVs under 17 CFR 270.2a-7 (``rule 
2a-7''). An amortized cost method of valuation values portfolio 
securities at their acquisition cost as adjusted for amortization of 
premium or accretion of discount, rather than valuing securities based 
on current market factors. Current rule 17a-7 requires cross trades to 
be effected at the ``current market price,'' and our proposed 
amendments similarly focus on market-based pricing. Money market funds 
that use the amortized cost method of valuation are separately required 
to calculate their NAVs using available market quotations (or an 
appropriate substitute that reflects current market conditions) at 
least daily, and they could use those NAV prices under the proposed NAV 
pricing approach.\62\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \62\ See 17 CFR 270.2a-7(g)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Registered funds relying on this approach would use the same 
pricing methodologies to determine the cross-trade price as they use 
for fund valuations. A fund would not be required to determine the 
cross-trade price separately, which should result in an efficient and 
cost-effective pricing process. This approach is designed to allow many 
cross trades to leverage existing processes.
    We propose the NAV pricing approach because it utilizes an existing 
methodology with robust processes, subject to rule 2a-5, to determine 
the price for the cross trade. These processes and controls would 
decrease the likelihood of inappropriate values for cross trading 
purposes and help address conflicts of interest while

[[Page 65630]]

preserving the benefits of cross trading, such as reduced execution 
costs. Further, because NAV pricing is derived from a fund's own 
valuation processes, which are themselves already subject to 
significant board oversight and scrutiny, this pricing method benefits 
from the same rigor and independence that governs the fund's broader 
valuation framework.\63\ This is expected to provide an additional 
layer of protection against conflicts of interest that can incentivize 
pricing a cross trade to the disadvantage of the registered fund and 
its shareholders relative to the eligible affiliate. In addition, 
because NAV pricing relies on the fund's valuation processes, we would 
expect any improvements to valuation techniques to apply to NAV 
pricing, which would improve cross trade pricing over time.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \63\ See, e.g., Valuation Rule Adopting Release, supra note 15, 
at nn.191-220 and accompanying text (outlining guidance on board 
oversight of the valuation process).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

2. Current Market Pricing
    Additionally, we propose to amend rule 17a-7 to provide that a 
cross trade could be effected at a price determined by the registered 
fund's investment adviser to reasonably represent current market price 
for the security using one or more unaffiliated pricing sources, 
provided that the adviser periodically reviews the reasonableness of 
such prices.\64\ Similar to the valuation process underlying NAV 
pricing, current market pricing may take into account multiple inputs 
and sources of data. Additionally, current market pricing may be used 
at any time, including intra-day, unlike NAV pricing, which would be 
determined by the registered fund's next computation of its NAV on the 
business day of the cross trade. The adviser, in using any unaffiliated 
pricing source, first would need to determine that the price reasonably 
represents the current market price for the security and also would 
need to periodically review the reasonableness of the prices used under 
this provision.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \64\ Proposed rule 17a-7(b)(2)(ii).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    We understand that it is not always practical or possible for 
registered funds to use NAV pricing to price cross trades. For example, 
a registered fund may wish to effect a cross trade intra-day, before 
the fund's next NAV computation, which is often at the close of 
business. Additionally, to analyze compliance with the rule's 
conditions, an adviser may find it more efficient to have all 
information about the potential cross trade, including pricing 
information, available at the time of the trade decision, instead of 
waiting for an end of day valuation process to be completed. As another 
example, for registered funds that do not compute their NAVs on a daily 
basis (e.g., some closed-end funds), a registered fund may wish to 
effect a cross trade on a day on which the fund will not compute its 
NAV. Using the current market pricing approach, the adviser might 
reasonably determine that using the same valuation methodology for the 
security as the fund would use if it were computing its NAV on that day 
would reasonably represent the current market price for the 
security.\65\ In these and other situations, allowing a registered 
fund's investment adviser to determine a cross-trade price that 
reasonably represents the current market price for the security using 
unaffiliated pricing sources would further promote the cost-saving 
benefits of cross trading while helping address conflicts of interest.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \65\ The registered fund, however, would not be required to 
value each of the securities in the registered fund or determine NAV 
for the registered fund in order to determine the price for the 
particular security being cross traded.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Determination That a Price Reasonably Represents the Current Market 
Price
    Using the proposed current market pricing approach, the registered 
fund's investment adviser would be required to determine the price that 
reasonably represents the current market price for the security being 
cross traded using one or more unaffiliated pricing sources. Consistent 
with funds' valuation methodologies and the current pricing provisions 
in rule 17a-7, the adviser's analysis of current market price and 
sources for unaffiliated pricing information would generally vary by 
asset type. A security with readily available market quotations must 
have quoted prices in active markets that the registered fund can 
access and that are reliable.\66\ For these securities, the adviser 
should look to the prices at which a particular security is being 
traded and quoted in active markets to determine a price that 
reasonably represents the current market price. For example, for cross 
trades of listed equity securities, it generally would be appropriate 
to use either the last reported sale price or, if there are no reported 
transactions on that day, the average of the highest current 
independent bid and the lowest current independent offer. This would be 
consistent with the current rule's asset-specific pricing requirements. 
Although we propose to remove these asset-specific pricing requirements 
in favor of standards that can be applied across permissible asset 
types, we do not intend for the proposed amendments to change how funds 
price cross trades of listed equity securities with readily available 
market quotations and continue to view the current rule's requirements 
as an appropriate way to comply with the proposal.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \66\ See rule 2a-5(c).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For securities that do not have readily available market 
quotations, a registered fund's investment adviser would use observable 
inputs from one or more unaffiliated pricing sources to determine a 
price that reasonably represents the current market price for the 
security. Registered funds already use various unaffiliated pricing 
sources, such as pricing services that provide evaluated prices by 
using matrix or model-based pricing methodologies, to support their NAV 
determinations. Broker-dealer quotes may continue to provide valuable 
pricing inputs. In addition, newer and developing sources, such as 
electronic trading platforms, may provide observable inputs to help 
determine price for some asset types, and we also understand that some 
pricing services are offering intra-day evaluated prices. These 
available unaffiliated pricing sources may be used by a registered 
fund's investment adviser to determine a price that reasonably 
represents the current market price for a cross trade. The proposal 
would also allow developing technologies and new unaffiliated pricing 
sources to be used.
    Under the proposal, the pricing sources an investment adviser uses 
would need to be unaffiliated. The proposed rule would define 
``unaffiliated'' to be a person other than an affiliated person or 
promoter of, or principal underwriter for, a fund (e.g., a first-tier 
affiliate) or an affiliated person of such entities (e.g., a second 
tier affiliate), consistent with the coverage of section 17(a).\67\ 
Requiring the pricing sources to be unaffiliated reduces the potential 
for conflicts of interest between the registered fund and the adviser 
and is designed to increase the likelihood that the terms of a cross 
trade are fair and reasonable to each participant and do not involve 
overreaching, consistent with section 17(b) of the Investment Company 
Act. The current rule similarly provides that cross trades must be 
effected at the independent current market price.\68\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \67\ See proposed rule 17a-7(d).
    \68\ See current rule 17a-7(b).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Regardless of the type of security or the unaffiliated pricing 
source used, the proposal would require the adviser to make a 
determination that the price of the cross trade reasonably represents 
the current market price for the security.

[[Page 65631]]

There are different ways an adviser might make this determination 
before executing a cross trade, and the approach may vary based on the 
type of security or the unaffiliated pricing source used. For example, 
an investment adviser considering the use of broker-dealer quotes as an 
unaffiliated pricing source generally should confirm with more than one 
broker-dealer that the quotes reflect current market conditions, are 
timely, are binding, and are verifiable (based on real transactions or 
other similar available quotes). These and any other appropriate 
factors would help inform an adviser's consideration of whether an 
average price based on the highest bid and lowest offer from the 
broker-dealers reasonably represents the current market price for the 
security. ``Indications of interest'' or ``accommodation quotes'' 
(i.e., non-firm expressions of interest to trade at a given price) 
would not reasonably represent the current market price of a security 
for purposes of cross trades under proposed rule 17a-7.\69\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \69\ This is consistent with prior Commission statements related 
to current rule 17a-7. See Investment Company Liquidity Risk 
Management Programs, Investment Company Act Release No. 32315 (Oct. 
13, 2016) [81 FR 82142 (Nov. 18, 2016)] (``Liquidity Rule Adopting 
Release'') at nn.800-801 and accompanying text.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Similarly, an investment adviser considering the use of prices from 
a pricing service as an unaffiliated pricing source, including for 
intra-day evaluated prices for securities that do not have readily 
available market quotations, should conduct due diligence on the 
service and its methodologies to determine whether prices provided by 
the service can be reasonably determined to represent current market 
value for the security. In this due diligence, an adviser could 
consider factors such as:
     The qualifications, experience, and history of the pricing 
service, particularly in providing intra-day pricing;
     The pricing methods or techniques, inputs, and assumptions 
the pricing service uses for different classes of holdings, how they 
are affected (if at all) as market conditions change, and, if the same 
pricing service is used for both NAV computation and current market 
pricing, how these methods or techniques may differ;
     The quality of the pricing information the service 
provides and the timing of the service's determination of pricing 
information relative to the timing of the cross trade;
     The pricing service's process for considering pricing 
challenges, including how the pricing service incorporates information 
received from pricing challenges into its pricing information;
     The pricing service's actual and potential conflicts of 
interest (e.g., potential conflicts associated with maintaining 
continuing business relationships and the potential incentive to 
provide higher or more aggressive prices to retain business) and the 
steps the pricing service takes to mitigate such conflicts; and
     The testing processes the pricing service uses, especially 
for newer technologies such as intra-day pricing information.\70\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \70\ See Valuation Rule Adopting Release, supra note 15, at 
paragraph accompanying n.117 (discussing similar factors for 
consideration when using pricing information provided by a pricing 
service in determining the fair values of the fund's investments).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Allowing registered funds' investment advisers to determine cross-
trade prices that reasonably represent current market prices using 
unaffiliated pricing sources such as pricing services and broker-dealer 
quotes is consistent with allowing registered funds to use these 
sources as part of a registered fund's NAV computation. In addition, 
improvements to the pricing process as a result of the adviser's 
evaluation of current market price could improve the NAV computation 
process.\71\ Similar to registered funds' valuation considerations, a 
registered fund relying on the current market pricing approach should 
select and apply in a consistent manner the methodologies the adviser 
uses to determine a price that reasonably represents the current market 
price.\72\ To the extent a fund uses the same pricing source for both 
NAV computation and current market pricing, it may combine the due 
diligence on the same vendor for both purposes and would not need to 
conduct a separate due diligence process.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \71\ The current market price may also be used as an input to a 
fair value measurement if the fund has evidence that the transaction 
was entered into at market terms. See Financial Accounting Standards 
Board (FASB), Master Glossary: Market Participant, at https://asc.fasb.org/MasterGlossary.
    \72\ See rule 2a-5(a)(2) (requiring that, for purposes of fair 
value determinations, a registered fund select and apply in a 
consistent manner an appropriate methodology or methodologies for 
determining (and calculating) the fair value of fund investments, 
provided that a selected methodology may be changed if a different 
methodology is equally or more representative of the fair value of 
fund investments, including specifying the key inputs and 
assumptions specific to each asset class or portfolio holding).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Reviewing the Reasonableness of Prices
    Under the proposed current market pricing approach, the registered 
fund's investment adviser would be required to periodically review the 
reasonableness of the prices. This review requirement is designed to 
ensure that prices determined under the current market pricing approach 
are reasonable and subject to appropriate oversight through periodic 
reviews.
    We are not proposing to require a particular method of reviewing 
cross-trade prices determined using the current market pricing approach 
or the frequency at which these reviews must occur. The investment 
adviser's review of the prices determined under the current market 
pricing approach for reasonableness would be established by the 
investment adviser and should be specific to the circumstances of the 
registered fund's cross trading, the type of security being cross 
traded, and the frequency and volume of cross-trading activity.
    When structuring the method and frequency of reviewing cross-trade 
prices under the current market pricing approach, it would be 
reasonable to consider the methods for reviewing a fund's valuations 
for purposes of NAV computations and whether applying such methods (or 
similar methods) would be appropriate for these purposes. For example, 
under rule 2a-5, funds must periodically review the appropriateness and 
accuracy of the fair value methodologies selected and make any 
necessary changes or adjustments to them, test the appropriateness and 
accuracy of fair value methodologies, and evaluate pricing services if 
used.\73\ These types of reviews could potentially be leveraged to 
review the reasonableness of prices used under the current market 
pricing approach. For example, if a specific approach to determining 
cross-trade prices consistently over- or under-prices securities as 
compared to observed market transactions or valuations used for NAV 
purposes, the adviser should investigate the reason for the difference 
and consider whether use of that approach for pricing cross trades 
continues to be reasonable.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \73\ See rule 2a-5(a)(2)(ii), (3), and (4).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Under the proposed rule, the registered fund's adviser would be 
responsible for conducting the periodic review of the reasonableness of 
prices used under the current market pricing approach. This review 
requirement would be separate from CCO review requirements in the 
proposal, which are more focused on reviewing cross trades for 
compliance with the rule, although the periodic reviews would be within 
the scope of the CCO's overall compliance assessments as well. We

[[Page 65632]]

propose to require the adviser to conduct this pricing review because 
the adviser overall is better situated to review the reasonableness of 
cross-trade prices than fund CCOs, as these reviews would involve 
considerations about available market data, and the choice of and 
reliability of different pricing sources. In addition, the adviser may 
be able to react more accurately and quickly to correct pricing issues 
than the CCO. This review is similar to the reviews that advisers may 
conduct for purposes of fund valuations.
    As discussed below, the proposed rule would require the retention 
of the information or materials upon which the CCO makes certain 
compliance-related determinations. This recordkeeping requirement would 
include information or materials used to determine that the pricing 
conditions of the proposed rule are satisfied.\74\ These records are 
designed so that a CCO would have the necessary information to review 
whether and how the investment adviser determined that the price 
reasonably represents the current market price, as well as the periodic 
review of the reasonableness of prices.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \74\ See proposed rule 17a-7(c)(2); see also infra section II.G 
(discussing the proposed recordkeeping requirements).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    We request comment on the proposed pricing requirements for cross 
trades.
    7. Are the proposed methodologies for pricing cross trades workable 
in practice?
    8. Would registered funds participating in cross trades receive a 
fair and reasonable independent current market price for the securities 
involved under the proposed pricing methodologies?
    9. Should we permit registered funds to use either the NAV pricing 
approach or the current market pricing approach for a cross trade, as 
proposed? Should a registered fund be permitted to switch between one 
pricing methodology and another for different cross trades, as 
proposed? Are the proposed approaches sufficiently evergreen? Would 
these approaches have any issues in an extended trading hours 
environment? Are there other ongoing or reasonably anticipated market 
developments that may raise issues with the proposed approach?
    10. Should we alternatively require cross trades to be priced under 
a single standard, or different standard(s) than those proposed? If so, 
would NAV pricing, current market pricing, or some other standard be 
most appropriate for a uniform approach? Should we permit more than two 
approaches to pricing? How would we ensure that investors are protected 
using those methods given the conflict of interest implicated by cross 
trading? What are the advantages and disadvantages to each method?
    11. Do the NAV pricing approach and the current market pricing 
approach work for all assets that registered funds would be permitted 
to cross trade under rule 17a-7? Should we have more specific pricing 
provisions based on, for example: how a security is traded, like the 
current rule; asset type (e.g., such as equities or fixed income, or 
level 1 or level 2 securities, to recognize differences in pricing 
sources); type of fund (e.g., such as closed-end or open-end); or some 
other method? Commission staff no-action letters have addressed pricing 
cross trades for certain types of securities, including municipal 
securities and variable rate demand notes (``VRDNs'').\75\ Are the 
proposed pricing provisions workable for these types of securities, or 
would registered funds need different conditions or guidance to 
facilitate pricing cross trades for these securities?
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \75\ See, e.g., Federated No-Action Letter (providing that the 
staff would not recommend enforcement action if cross trades of 
municipal securities that lack readily available market quotations 
are conducted at a price provided by an independent pricing service 
that values the fund's municipal securities for purposes of 
determining the fund's net asset value); Benham California Tax Free 
Trust and Benham National Tax-Free Trust, SEC Staff No-Action Letter 
(Aug. 6, 1986) (providing that the staff would not recommend 
enforcement action if cross trades of VRDNs are priced at par plus 
accrued interest).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    12. Are there circumstances in which either NAV pricing or current 
market pricing should not be permitted? For example, we understand that 
some registered funds value portfolio investments at the bid price, 
rather than the mid price, when computing their NAVs.\76\ Rule 17a-7 
currently requires that cross trades be executed at mid prices. Should 
registered funds that price at bid be permitted to cross trade at the 
bid price under NAV pricing when doing so aligns with the valuation of 
the security or should they use current market pricing? Is using NAV 
pricing at bid fair and reasonable for the seller in the cross trade, 
even though it is receiving a lower price than it would if mid prices 
were used? What would be the advantages and disadvantages of allowing 
cross trades to occur at bid prices under the NAV pricing approach? For 
example, the seller would not avoid spread costs under these 
circumstances but might avoid other costs associated with open market 
transactions (e.g., market impact) and experience reduced risks (e.g., 
counterparty or liquidity risk).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \76\ See ASC 820-10-35-36C. GAAP provides that if an asset 
measured at fair value has a bid price and an ask price (for 
example, an input from a dealer market), the price within the bid-
ask spread that is most representative of fair value in the 
circumstances shall be used to measure fair value, and that the use 
of bid prices for asset positions is permitted but not required for 
these purposes. Id.; see also ASC-820-10-35-36D (stating that use of 
mid-market pricing as a practical expedient for fair value 
measurements within a bid-ask spread is not precluded). Mid-market 
pricing values a security at the average of its bid and ask prices. 
Since a seller generally asks for a higher price for a security than 
a buyer bids for that security, the mid-market price is higher than 
the bid price for a security, but lower than its ask price.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    13. Under the proposed NAV pricing approach, the execution price 
for a cross trade would not be known until the registered fund's next 
NAV computation on that business day, which may be at the end of the 
day or during the day for funds that make multiple NAV computations 
during a business day. Would this create operational or practical 
impediments to using the NAV pricing approach? If so, would these 
impediments occur in specific scenarios (e.g., with particular types of 
cross-trade counterparties) or for particular types of registered 
funds, or would the impediments be broader based for registered funds? 
How would registered funds weigh any such impediments against the 
efficiencies that the NAV pricing approach may present?
    14. How should funds that compute their NAVs less frequently or 
more frequently than daily price cross trades? Should the funds that 
compute their NAV less frequently than daily be able to use NAV pricing 
only on the days that they perform NAV computations, as proposed? 
Should these funds be allowed to use NAV pricing by following their NAV 
pricing procedures to price cross trades on days the funds do not 
compute their NAVs? Are there any impediments to using the next NAV 
computation for funds that make more than one NAV computation daily?
    15. How should money market funds that use the amortized cost 
method of valuation under rule 2a-7 implement NAV pricing to price a 
cross trade? Should these funds be required to use their market-based 
NAV prices, as proposed, or should they be able to use the amortized 
cost value of a security for cross trades?
    16. Rule 2a-4 under the Investment Company Act permits funds to 
reflect changes in holdings of portfolio securities in fund NAVs on the 
next business day. As a result, registered funds currently may not 
value newly acquired securities on the day of acquisition. How would 
this affect the use of NAV pricing for cross trades?
    17. Under the current market pricing approach, should we permit the 
registered fund's adviser to determine a

[[Page 65633]]

price that reasonably represents the current market price using one or 
more unaffiliated pricing sources, as proposed? Do advisers need 
additional requirements or guidance on how to make these 
determinations? Please provide specific information on what 
requirements or guidance would be helpful and how. For example, are 
there circumstances when listed equity securities would not be priced 
using the last reported sale price or, if there are no reported 
transactions on that day, the average of the highest current 
independent bid and the lowest current independent offer? If so, what 
are they, and how would the adviser determine a price?
    18. What unaffiliated pricing sources would an investment adviser 
use to determine the price that reasonably represents the current 
market price for a security under the proposed methodology? Should the 
rule or Commission guidance address the use of particular pricing 
sources, for example, electronic trading platforms? If so, how? How are 
unaffiliated pricing sources offering intra-day information (for 
example, for which asset classes, at what frequency, and using what 
delivery method)?
    19. Should a pricing source be required to be unaffiliated, as 
proposed? Should we, as proposed, define ``unaffiliated'' as persons 
other than first- or second-tier affiliates? Should a fund be permitted 
to use a pricing source that is affiliated with the registered fund or 
investment adviser to determine the current market price under certain
