full_text:
Outside Activities
Summary
FINRA has adopted new Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements) to replace Rules 3270 (Outside Business Activities of Registered Persons) and 3280 (Private Securities Transactions of an Associated Person). Rule 3290 consolidates and streamlines the requirements governing registered persons’ outside activities and associated persons' outside securities transactions.
The effective date of Rule 3290 is October 25, 2027.
The rule text is available in Attachment A. A flowchart illustrating the rule text is available in Attachment B.
Questions concerning this Notice may be directed to:
- Alicia Goldin, Vice President and Associate General Counsel, Office of General Counsel (OGC), by email or (202) 728-8155;
- Micah Hauptman, Associate General Counsel, OGC, by email or (202) 728-8123; or
- Matthew Vitek, Associate General Counsel, OGC, by email or (240) 386-6490.
Background & Discussion
New Rule 3290 is part of the FINRA Forward initiative, which is intended to modernize FINRA's rules, guidance and processes, and empower member compliance.1 FINRA Forward reflects FINRA's commitment to reducing unnecessary burdens on members while maintaining core investor protections. Rule 3290 replaces Rules 3270 and 3280 with a single, consolidated framework governing investment-related activities and securities transactions outside the scope of an associated person's relationship with a member.2
Existing Rule 3270 prohibits a registered person from being an employee, independent contractor, sole proprietor, officer, director or partner of another person, or being compensated, or having the reasonable expectation of compensation, from any other person as a result of any business activity outside the scope of the relationship with his or her member, unless he or she has provided prior written notice to the member.
Upon receiving notice, the member must assess whether the proposed activity will: (1) interfere with or otherwise compromise the registered person's responsibilities to the member or the member's customers; or (2) be viewed by customers or the public as part of the member's business based upon, among other factors, the nature of the proposed activity and the manner in which it will be offered. Based on that assessment, the member must evaluate whether to impose conditions or limitations on the activity, including, where circumstances warrant, prohibiting it.
The member also must assess whether a registered person’s activity properly is characterized as an outside business activity or whether it should be treated as a private securities transaction subject to the requirements of Rule 3280. A private securities transaction is a securities transaction outside the regular course or scope of an associated person’s employment with a member.
Existing Rule 3280 requires an associated person, prior to participating in any private securities transaction, to provide written notice to the member describing in detail the proposed transaction and the person's proposed role, and stating whether the associated person has received or may receive selling compensation. The member's obligations depend on whether the transaction involves selling compensation. For transactions not involving selling compensation, the member must provide prompt written acknowledgment of the notice and may, at its discretion, impose conditions. For transactions involving selling compensation, the member must advise the associated person in writing whether it approves or disapproves participation. If approved, the member must record the transaction on its books and records and supervise the associated person's participation as if the transaction were executed on behalf of the member.
In addition, through a series of Notices to Members issued in the 1990s, FINRA applied Rule 3280's requirements to outside investment advisory (IA) activities, treating certain IA activity as participation in private securities transactions subject to member supervision and recordkeeping.3 Rule 3290 changes this treatment, as described below under “Activity at an Unaffiliated Registered Investment Adviser.”
Activities Subject to New Rule 3290
Rule 3290 distinguishes between an “outside activity” and an “outside securities transaction.” Rule 3290 maintains the existing bifurcated approach of Rules 3270 and 3280: outside activities requirements apply to registered persons, while outside securities transaction requirements apply to all associated persons, including registered persons.
Pursuant to Rule 3290(a), an outside activity is an investment-related activity outside the scope of a registered person’s relationship with a member that is not in connection with a securities transaction. A registered person intending to participate in an outside activity must provide prior written notice to the member. The notice must describe in detail the proposed activity and the registered person’s proposed role. The registered person must provide updated prior written notice if there is a material change to the activity.
Under Rule 3290(b)(1), an outside securities transaction is an investment-related activity outside the scope of an associated person’s relationship with a member that is in connection with a securities transaction. An associated person intending to participate in an outside securities transaction must provide prior written notice to the member. For an outside securities transaction involving selling compensation, the associated person must also obtain the member’s prior written approval. As required by Rule 3290(b)(3), the notice must describe in detail the proposed transaction, series of related transactions, the person’s proposed role and whether the person will receive selling compensation. And, pursuant to Rule 3290(b)(2), an associated person must provide updated prior written notice, and in the case of an outside securities transaction for selling compensation, obtain updated prior written approval if there is a material change to the information previously provided.
Rule 3290(b)(1)(A) and (B) permit a single prior written notice where: (1) an associated person intends to participate in an outside securities transaction in connection with a series of related securities transactions not for selling compensation; or (2) an associated person acting as portfolio manager or investment committee member (as described in Supplementary Material .02) is not selling an entity's shares for selling compensation.
Investment-Related Activity
Rule 3290(f)(3) defines “investment-related activity” as activity pertaining to financial assets, including, but not limited to, securities, crypto assets, commodities, derivatives (such as futures and swaps), currency, banking, real estate or insurance.
Under Rule 3290(f)(3)(A), the term includes, but is not limited to, acting as or being associated with a broker-dealer; issuer; insurance agent or company; investment company; investment adviser; futures commission merchant; commodity trading advisor; commodity pool operator; municipal advisor; futures sponsor; money services business; bank; savings association; or credit union.
Rule 3290(f)(3)(B) also includes within the definition an associated person’s participation in any manner in a personal investment involving a securities transaction, sometimes referred to as “buying away,” unless the transaction is excluded under Rule 3290(g)(3)(A).
Even if not expressly listed among the examples in the definition, activities pertaining to financial assets and other related roles or associations would be covered.4
By focusing on investment-related activities, Rule 3290 eliminates the rule-based requirement to report and assess lower-risk, non-investment-related activities, such as refereeing sports games, driving for a car service or bartending on weekends.5
Members’ Assessment Obligations
Pursuant to Rules 3290(c)(1) and 3290(d)(1), upon receiving written notice of a registered person’s outside activity or an associated person’s outside securities transaction, a member generally must assess, at a minimum, whether the activity:
- is properly characterized, because the member’s obligations depend on whether the activity is an outside activity, an outside securities transaction or an outside securities transaction for selling compensation;
- involves a customer of the registered or associated person;
- will interfere with or otherwise compromise the registered or associated person’s responsibilities to the member or the member’s customers; and
- will be viewed by the member’s customers or the public as part of the member’s business, based upon, among other factors, the nature of the activity and the manner in which it will be offered.
A member is not required to conduct the assessment under Rule 3290(d)(1) if it disapproves an outside securities transaction for selling compensation under Rule 3290(d)(3)(C).
These assessment factors are consistent with the existing requirements under Rule 3270 for an outside business activity. The one new factor requires the member to consider whether the activity or transaction involves a customer of the registered person or associated person.
Under Rule 3290, as under the existing rules, the member’s obligations differ depending on the type of activity or transaction.
- Under Rule 3290(c)(2), for a registered person’s outside activity, the member must evaluate whether to impose specific conditions or limitations on the outside activity, including where circumstances warrant, prohibiting the activity, but there is no acknowledgement or approval requirement.
- Under Rule 3290(d)(2), for an associated person’s outside securities transaction not for selling compensation, the member must provide the associated person prompt written acknowledgement of the notice and may, at the member’s discretion, require the associated person to adhere to specified conditions or limitations in connection with the associated person’s participation in the transaction, but there is no approval requirement.
- Under Rule 3290(d)(3), for an associated person's outside securities transaction for selling compensation, the member must notify the associated person in writing of its decision to: (A) approve the proposed transaction after making a reasonable determination based on the assessment criteria; (B) approve the proposed transaction subject to specific conditions or limitations after making a reasonable determination based on the assessment criteria; or (C) disapprove the proposed transaction. Pursuant to Rule 3290(d)(4), if the member approves the proposed transaction, it must record each transaction on its books and records and supervise the associated person's participation as if the transaction were executed on behalf of the member.
Rule 3290.06 requires a member that imposes conditions or limitations on an outside activity or an outside securities transaction to reasonably supervise compliance with such conditions or limitations.
Rule 3290 does not restrict a member’s ability to establish broader internal reporting or approval requirements, or to limit, condition, or prohibit any outside activity or outside securities transaction based on the member’s own risk management considerations. Nor does Rule 3290 alter a member’s supervisory obligations under applicable federal law or under Rule 3110, including its responsibility to investigate and respond appropriately to “red flags” suggesting an undisclosed outside activity or securities transaction, undisclosed compensation or other misconduct.6
Exclusions
Rule 3290 does not apply to the following activities and transactions:
Activity on Behalf of a Member or Affiliate
Rule 3290(g)(1) excludes activity conducted on behalf of a member or its affiliate. This exclusion includes, for example, investment advisory activity conducted for a dually registered broker-dealer and investment adviser, and investment advisory, insurance or banking activity conducted at an affiliate of the member. Rule 3290(f)(1) defines an “affiliate” as any entity that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with a member.
Immediate Family Transactions
Rule 3290(g)(2) excludes securities transactions among immediate family members where the associated person receives no selling compensation. Rule 3290(f)(2) defines “immediate family” by reference to Rule 3240(c). Under that definition, “immediate family” means parents, grandparents, a mother-in-law or father-in-law, a spouse or domestic partner, a brother or sister, a brother-in-law or sister-in-law, a son-in-law or daughter-in-law, children, grandchildren, a cousin, an aunt or uncle, or a niece or nephew. The term also includes step and adoptive relationships, as well as any other person who resides in the same household as the registered person and whom the registered person financially supports, directly or indirectly, to a material extent.
Specified Personal Investments
Rule 3290(g)(3) excludes the following personal investments:
- securities transactions subject to or delineated in Rule 3210 (e.g., securities held at other members, as well as transactions in certain securities, such as mutual funds, Section 529 plans and variable annuities);7
- personal investments in non-securities; and
- the purchase, sale, rental or lease of a main home and up to two secondary homes that are:
  - solely owned by the associated person or the associated person and immediate family;
  - owned by the associated person as a sole proprietorship;
  - owned by a corporation, LLC, partnership, limited partnership, or other entity that is solely owned by the associated person or the associated person and immediate family; or
  - owned by a trust with the associated person or the associated person and immediate family as the sole beneficiaries.
Rule 3290(f)(4) defines a “secondary home” as property used for residential purposes by the associated person for at least part of the year.
Special Treatment
Activity at an Unaffiliated Registered Investment Adviser
Rule 3290 significantly changes the treatment of an associated person’s activity at an unaffiliated investment adviser registered with the SEC or a state securities commission.
Under current FINRA guidance issued in the 1990s, certain outside investment advisory activities are treated as private securities transactions subject to a member's supervision and recordkeeping obligations. Under Rule 3290.03, activity at an unaffiliated SEC- or state-registered investment adviser is considered an outside activity of a registered person, rather than an outside securities transaction.
Accordingly, under Rules 3290(a) and (c), a registered person must provide prior written notice of the activity, and the member must perform the assessment required for outside activities. The member is no longer required under Rule 3290 to supervise or maintain records of the investment advisory activity itself, although it must maintain records demonstrating its compliance with Rule 3290. As mentioned above, if the member imposes conditions or limitations on the activity, however, the member must reasonably supervise the registered person’s compliance with those conditions or limitations.
This treatment applies only to activity at an investment adviser registered with the SEC under Section 203 of the Investment Advisers Act or a state securities commission (or any agency or office performing like functions). As noted above, it does not alter a member’s responsibility to investigate and respond appropriately to “red flags” suggesting undisclosed activity or other misconduct.
Notwithstanding the elimination of supervision and recordkeeping obligations for unaffiliated registered investment adviser activity, members retain full discretion to impose conditions or limitations on such activity, including subjecting it to member supervision, based on their assessment of the associated risk. Nothing in Rule 3290 limits a member's ability to impose additional oversight of outside activities at its discretion.
Upon Rule 3290’s effective date, the guidance in Notices to Members 94-44 and 96-33 regarding the treatment of outside investment advisory activities as private securities transactions subject to member supervision and recordkeeping obligations is superseded.
Portfolio Managers and Investment Committee Members
Rule 3290.02 provides that specified activity as a portfolio manager or investment committee member is treated as an outside activity of a registered person rather than an outside securities transaction of an associated person. This treatment applies to activities limited to acting as portfolio manager or investment committee member for registered investment companies (e.g., mutual funds, exchange traded funds, unit investment trusts, registered closed-end funds), unregistered investment companies, business development companies, real estate investment trusts and entities that are recognized as tax exempt.
This treatment does not apply to an associated person’s activity involving the purchase or sale of the entity’s shares, unless the activity is otherwise excluded under Rule 3290.
Contractual Arrangements
Rule 3290.04 provides that an associated person’s activity pursuant to a contract between a member and another entity, such as a banking or insurance networking arrangement, is not subject to Rule 3290 if the activity is conducted on behalf of the member and is within the scope of the associated person’s relationship with the member.
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and Regulation R Activity
Rule 3290.05 provides that securities activity qualifying for an exception from broker or dealer registration under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act or SEC Regulation R is treated as an outside activity rather than an outside securities transaction, unless it is covered by the contractual arrangement provision in Rule 3290.04.
Formal Allocation Agreements
If a person associated with more than one member engages in an approved outside securities transaction involving selling compensation, Rule 3290.01 permits the members to enter into a written allocation agreement under which at least one member assumes responsibility for compliance with applicable securities laws, regulations and FINRA rules regarding the proposed activity, including supervision and recordkeeping requirements.
Recordkeeping
Under Rule 3290(e), a member must maintain records demonstrating its compliance with Rule 3290 and preserve those records for the period and in the manner specified in Exchange Act Rule 17a-4(e)(1).
Exemptive Relief
Rule 3290(h) permits a member to apply for exemptive relief under the Rule 9600 Series. For good cause shown, FINRA staff may grant a conditional or unconditional exemption from any provision of Rule 3290 after considering all relevant factors to the extent that such exemption is consistent with the purposes of the rule, investor protection and the public interest.
Rule 9610 is amended to add Rule 3290 to the rules for which a member may seek exemptive relief.
Endnotes
1 See FINRA Forward: A Year of Progress (April 2026).
2 See Securities Exchange Act Release No. 106381 (September 15, 2026), 91 FR 59259 (September 18, 2026) (Order Approving a Proposed Rule Change, as Modified by Partial Amendment No. 1, To Adopt FINRA Rule 3290 (Outside Activities Requirements)) (“Approval Order”).
3 See Notice to Members 94-44 (May 1994); Notice to Members 96-33 (May 1996).
4 Although consulting, marketing, accounting, legal and tax advice standing alone would not be covered (e.g., assistance with tax returns), such services that are concomitant to investment-related activity would be covered. For example, recommending the sale of a security for a loss for tax purposes or recommending the purchase of an investment in a tax-advantaged account would be considered investment-related activity.
5 FINRA notes that Rule 3290 does not alter existing Form U4 disclosure obligations. Question 13 (“Other Business”) in Form U4 requires disclosure about outside activities.
6 See Approval Order, 91 FR 59265, 59268, 59274–75; letter from Matthew E. Vitek, associate general counsel, FINRA, to Vanessa Countryman, secretary, SEC, at 13 & nn. 37–38 (May 1, 2026).
7 Rule 3210 applies to accounts opened or maintained by an associated person at another member or financial institution in which the associated person has a beneficial interest. Rule 3210.03 delineates transactions and accounts not subject to the rule (“The requirements of this Rule shall not apply to transactions in unit investment trusts, municipal fund securities as defined under MSRB Rule D-12, qualified tuition programs pursuant to Section 529 of the Internal Revenue Code and variable contracts or redeemable securities of companies registered under the Investment Company Act, as amended, or to accounts that are limited to transactions in such securities, or to Monthly Investment Plan type accounts or accounts pursuant to Section 530A of the Internal Revenue Code.”).

title: Regulatory Notice 26-19
abstract: Summary FINRA has amended Rules 5110 (Corporate Financing Rule – Underwriting Terms and Arrangements) and 5123 (Private Placements of Securities) to make substantive, organizational and terminology changes to the rules. 1 These amendments simplify and clarify rule provisions while maintaining important protections for market participants, including issuers and investors participating in public offerings.

title: Regulatory Notice 26-18
abstract: Summary FINRA has adopted amendments to Rule 1210.06 (Waiting Periods for Retaking a Failed Examination) that shorten the retake waiting periods for FINRA qualification examinations from 30 calendar days to 15 calendar days after the first and second failed attempts, and from 180 calendar days to 60 calendar days after the third and any subsequent failed attempts within a two-year period. The amendments will become effective on January 19, 2027.

title: [Rule] Imposition of Special Measure Prohibiting the Transmittal of Funds Involving MEXC Global
abstract: FinCEN is issuing notice of an order, pursuant to section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act (Pub. L. 116- 283), as amended by section 6106(b) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (Pub. L. 117-81), finding that MEXC Global--including any of its subsidiaries, branches, and offices, as well as any successor entities, operating in any jurisdiction outside of the United States--is a financial institution operating outside of the United States of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance and prohibiting certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global.
full_text:
[Federal Register Volume 91, Number 216 (Tuesday, November 10, 2026)]
[Rules and Regulations]
[Pages 72420-72427]
From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [www.gpo.gov]
[FR Doc No: 2026-22962]


=======================================================================
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY

Financial Crimes Enforcement Network

31 CFR Part 1010


Imposition of Special Measure Prohibiting the Transmittal of 
Funds Involving MEXC Global

AGENCY: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Treasury.

ACTION: Order.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: FinCEN is issuing notice of an order, pursuant to section 
9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act (Pub. L. 116-
283), as amended by section 6106(b) of the National Defense 
Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (Pub. L. 117-81), finding that 
MEXC Global--including any of its subsidiaries, branches, and offices, 
as well as any successor entities, operating in any jurisdiction 
outside of the United States--is a financial institution operating 
outside of the United States of primary money laundering concern in 
connection with Russian illicit finance and prohibiting certain 
transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global.

DATES: This action is effective December 10, 2026.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: FinCEN's Regulatory Support Section by 
submitting an inquiry at www.fincen.gov/contact.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Summary of Order

    As set out in this order, MEXC Global has facilitated funds 
transfers by Russia-affiliated illicit actors and in connection with 
other Russia-associated illicit activities, including sanctions 
evasion, and activity facilitated by Russian darknet markets. It has 
also facilitated billions of dollars in transactions benefitting Iran 
and its proxies, financial facilitators of the Democratic People's 
Republic of Korea (DPRK), and other cybercrime actors. Accordingly, 
this order (1) sets forth FinCEN's determination that MEXC Global, a 
convertible virtual currency (CVC) exchanger, along with any 
subsidiaries, branches, and offices of MEXC Global, and any successor 
entities, operating in any jurisdiction outside of the United States 
(collectively, MEXC Global) \1\ is a financial institution operating 
outside of the United States of primary money laundering concern in 
connection with Russian illicit finance; and (2) prohibits certain 
transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global, by any covered financial 
institution.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ This includes, but is not limited to, active and past MEXC 
affiliated entities MEXC Global Ltd/MX Global Ltd (Seychelles); MEXC 
Estonia O[Uuml] (Estonia); GIDA Technology AG (Switzerland); and MXC 
Global Ltd (United Kingdom); affiliated entities formerly 
incorporated in Singapore MEXC Global Foundation Ltd and MEXC 
Singapore Pte Ltd; and any successor entities.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

II. Background

A. Statutory Provisions

    Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act (Pub. 
L. 116-283), as amended by section 6106(b) of the National Defense 
Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (Pub. L. 117-81) (section 
9714),\2\ provides, in relevant part, that, if the Secretary of the 
Treasury (Secretary) ``determines that reasonable grounds exist for 
concluding that one or more financial institutions operating outside of 
the United States . . . is of primary money laundering concern in 
connection with Russian illicit finance,'' the Secretary may, ``by 
order, regulation, or otherwise as permitted by law'': (1) require 
domestic financial institutions and domestic financial agencies to take 
one or more of the special measures described in 31 U.S.C. 5318A(b); 
\3\ or (2) prohibit, or impose conditions upon, certain transmittals of 
funds (as defined by the Secretary) by any domestic financial 
institution or domestic financial agency (collectively, covered 
financial institutions), if such transmittal of funds involves any such 
financial institution. The authority of the Secretary to administer 
both section 9714 and the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) has been delegated to 
FinCEN.\4\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \2\ Section 9714 (as amended) may be found in a note to 31 
U.S.C. 5318A.
    \3\ See infra note [4].
    \4\ Pursuant to Treasury Order 180-01, the authority of the 
Secretary of the Treasury (Secretary) to administer the BSA, 
including, but not limited to, 31 U.S.C. 5318A, has been delegated 
to the Director of FinCEN. Treasury Order 180-01 (Jan. 14, 2020). On 
August 11, 2022, and in accordance with Treasury Order 101-05 and 31 
U.S.C. 321(b), Treasury's Under Secretary for Terrorism & Financial 
Intelligence re-delegated to the Director of FinCEN the authority of 
the Secretary under section 9714.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Pursuant to section 9714, the Secretary may impose one or more of 
six special measures. First, the Secretary may impose any of the five 
special measures provided for in 31 U.S.C. 5318A(b), commonly known as 
section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act.\5\ Through special measures one 
through four, the Secretary may impose additional recordkeeping, 
information collection, and reporting requirements on covered financial 
institutions.\6\ Through special measure five, the Secretary, in 
consultation with the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, and the 
Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, may 
``prohibit, or impose conditions upon, the opening or maintaining in 
the United States of a correspondent account or payable-through 
account'' for or on behalf of a foreign banking institution, if such 
correspondent account or payable-through account involves the financial 
institution operating outside of the United States found to be of 
primary money laundering concern.\7\ In addition

[[Page 72421]]

to the special measures set out in 31 U.S.C. 5318A, section 9714 also 
provides that the Secretary may impose a special measure prohibiting, 
or imposing conditions upon, certain transmittals of funds.\8\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \5\ See 31 U.S.C. 5318A. 31 U.S.C. 5318A grants the Secretary 
the authority, upon finding that reasonable grounds exist for 
concluding that one or more financial institutions operating outside 
of the United States is of primary money laundering concern, to 
require domestic financial institutions and domestic financial 
agencies to take certain ``special measures.'' Regarding the 
``special measures'' that might be imposed, section 9714 references 
the five special measures set out in 31 U.S.C. 5318A(b)(1)-(5).
    \6\ 31 U.S.C. 5318A(b)(1)-(4).
    \7\ 31 U.S.C. 5318A(b)(5).
    \8\ See section 9714(a)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

B. MEXC Global

    MEXC Global is a CVC exchanger founded in 2018 that is incorporated 
in the Seychelles, without a virtual asset service provider license \9\ 
and operates in and across over 170 countries \10\ through an array of 
current or former subsidiaries, branches, and offices, including, but 
not limited to, MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles; MEXC 
Estonia O[Uuml] in Estonia; GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland; MXC 
Global Ltd in the United Kingdom; and, formerly, Singapore-registered 
MEXC Global Foundation Ltd and MEXC Singapore Pte Ltd.\11\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \9\ See Financial Services Authority Seychelles, Press Release--
FSA Takes Enforcement Action Against MX Global Ltd for Unlicensed 
Virtual Asset Services Operations (May 26, 2026), https://fsaseychelles.sc/news/press-releases/fsa-takes-enforcement-action-against-mx-global-ltd-for-unlicensed-virtual-asset-services-operations.
    \10\ See CoinPedia, MEXC Overview, https://app.coinpedia.org/company/mexc/.
    \11\ TRM Labs, MEXC Global (accessed Jun. 3, 2026). MEXC Global 
was formerly known as MXC before rebranding in 2021. See MEXC 
Global, ``MXC Exchange Rebranded MEXC Global, Deepening its Global 
Compliance Strategy,'' Medium (June 10, 2021).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    As of June 2026, MEXC Global processed more than USD 1 billion in 
daily transactions, while maintaining approximately USD 5 billion in 
reserve assets. As such, MEXC Global is among the 20 largest CVC 
exchangers in the world by trading volume.\12\ As of December 2025, 
MEXC Global commanded approximately nine percent of the global market 
share of centralized CVC exchangers by trading volume.\13\ By 
comparison, the assets of the two largest centralized CVC exchangers 
together represented 47.4 percent of the global market share.\14\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \12\ See CoinPedia, Top Crypto Exchanges By Trading Volume, 
https://markets.coinpedia.org/exchanges/.
    \13\ See CoinGecko, Market Share of Centralized Crypto 
Exchanges, by Trading Volume (May 2, 2026), https://www.coingecko.com/research/publications/centralized-crypto-exchanges-market-share.
    \14\ See CoinGecko, Market Share of Centralized Crypto 
Exchanges, by Trading Volume (May 2, 2026), https://www.coingecko.com/research/publications/centralized-crypto-exchanges-market-share.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    According to its user agreement, MEXC Global allows customers to 
open user accounts for exchange between various fiat currencies and 
CVC, as well as for futures trading and other services.\15\ And, 
according to non-public information available to FinCEN, as of July 
2026, MEXC Global offers the ability to trade in over fifty currencies, 
including USD and Russian rubles (RUB), as well as access to over 3,000 
different CVCs and tokenized assets.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \15\ See MEXC, User Agreement (May 29, 2025), https://www.mexc.com/terms.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

III. Finding That MEXC Global Is a Financial Institution Operating 
Outside the United States That Is of Primary Money Laundering Concern 
in Connection With Russian Illicit Finance

    Based on public and non-public information available to FinCEN, 
FinCEN finds that reasonable grounds exist for concluding that MEXC 
Global is a financial institution of primary money laundering concern 
in connection with Russian illicit finance--namely, through its 
facilitation of funds transfers by Russia-affiliated illicit actors and 
in connection with other Russia-associated illicit activities, 
including sanctions evasion, and activity facilitated by Russian 
darknet markets. Moreover, FinCEN assesses that, in addition to 
facilitating Russian illicit finance, MEXC Global has, in parallel, 
facilitated billions of dollars in transactions benefitting Iran and 
its proxies, financial facilitators of the Democratic People's Republic 
of Korea (DPRK), and other cybercrime actors.
    In making this finding, FinCEN has considered the relevant evidence 
in light of factors identified in 31 U.S.C. 5318A(c)(2)(B), taking into 
account the specific circumstances of money laundering activities in 
connection with Russian illicit finance and the protection of U.S. 
national security and the U.S. financial system. While FinCEN is under 
no obligation pursuant to section 9714 to consider any particular 
factor or set of factors when making a finding that a financial 
institution operating outside of the United States is of primary money 
laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance, it 
nonetheless finds these factors instructive in guiding the analysis set 
forth below.\16\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \16\ 31 U.S.C. 5318A(c)(2)(B) provides, as relevant here, that 
in making a finding that reasonable grounds exist for concluding 
that a class of transactions within, or involving, a jurisdiction 
outside the United States is of primary money laundering concern and 
to apply one or more of special measures one through four to such a 
financial institution, the Secretary shall consider such information 
as the Secretary determines to be relevant, including the following 
potentially relevant factors: (1) The extent to which such financial 
institutions, transactions, or types of accounts are used to 
facilitate or promote money laundering in or through the 
jurisdiction, including any money laundering activity by organized 
criminal groups, international terrorists, or entities involved in 
the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction or missiles; (2) 
The extent to which such institutions, transactions, or types of 
accounts are used for legitimate business purposes in the 
jurisdiction; and (3) The extent to which such action is sufficient 
to ensure, with respect to transactions involving the jurisdiction 
and institutions operating in the jurisdiction, that the purposes of 
this subchapter continue to be fulfilled, and to guard against 
international money laundering and other financial crimes.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. MEXC Global Is a Financial Institution Operating Outside the United 
States

    Although section 9714 does not expressly define the term 
``financial institution,'' FinCEN has long defined that term to include 
``money transmitters,'' including persons that accept and transmit 
value that substitutes for currency, such as CVC.\17\ MEXC Global, in 
operating as a CVC exchanger, is a ``money transmitter'' because it is 
engaged in the transfer of funds or value that substitutes for 
currency.\18\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \17\ See, e.g., 31 U.S.C. 5312; 31 CFR 1010.100(t)(3); 
1010.100(ff); 1010.605(f)(iv); FinCEN, FIN-2019-G001, Application of 
FinCEN's Regulations to Certain Business Models Involving 
Convertible Virtual Currencies (May 9, 2019); FinCEN, FIN-2013-G001, 
Application of FinCEN's Regulations to Persons Administering, 
Exchanging, or Using Virtual Currencies (Mar. 18, 2013); see also 31 
U.S.C. 5312(a)(2)(J).
    \18\ See 31 CFR 1010.100(t)(3), (ff)(5).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    By its own account and as described above, MEXC Global operates 
through affiliates throughout the world--over time maintaining, for 
instance, subsidiaries, branches, and offices in Seychelles, Hong Kong, 
Singapore, Estonia, and the United Kingdom--and offers a range of money 
transmitter services for individual and institutional customers in the 
CVC sector in over 170 countries.\19\ Considering the services that it 
provides and its places of registration, FinCEN assesses that MEXC 
Global is a financial institution operating outside of the United 
States within the meaning of section 9714.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Notably, to the extent that MEXC Global maintains or otherwise 
operates through affiliates, subsidiaries, branches, or offices in the 
United States, this order expressly excludes all such affiliates, 
subsidiaries, branches, or offices from the definition of ``MEXC 
Global'' and, accordingly, such affiliates, subsidiaries, branches, or 
offices are outside the scope of this order.

B. Finding That MEXC Global Is a Financial Institution of Primary Money 
Laundering Concern in Connection With Russian Illicit Finance

    While MEXC Global's anti-money laundering and countering the 
financing

of terrorism (AML/CFT), customer identification and verification 
(sometimes referred to as ``Know Your Customer'' or ``KYC'' 
information), and other due diligence processes \20\ prohibit, on 
paper, the opening of accounts by individuals in certain jurisdictions, 
FinCEN assesses that, based on public and non-public information, MEXC 
Global has facilitated transactions involving those prohibited 
jurisdictions. In addition, MEXC Global has facilitated transactions 
involving Russia-affiliated illicit actors and associated illicit 
activities, including sanctions evasion, and activity facilitated by 
Russian darknet markets, as well as transactions involving not only 
U.S.-, European Union-, and United Kingdom-sanctioned persons working 
on behalf of Iran and its proxies and the DPRK, but also an array of 
cybercrime actors.

1. MEXC Global Is Used in Furtherance of Sanctions Evasion in 
Connection With Russian Illicit Finance
    MEXC Global has a history of processing CVC transfers for multiple 
key actors that support Russian illicit finance. According to FinCEN 
analysis of blockchain data, between May 2021 and May 2026, MEXC Global 
sent or received nearly USD 1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure 
to transactions linked to Russian sanctions evasion and had significant 
exposure to Russian cyber actors connected to sanctions evasion and/or 
cybercrime. This includes USD 232 million in direct transactions with 
entities sanctioned by the United States, the European Union (EU), and/
or the United Kingdom (UK).\24\ For example, MEXC Global transacted 
with the sanctioned, Russia-backed CVC exchangers Garantex and Grinex. 
Between 2019 and 2025, Garantex facilitated the movement of over USD 
100 million for ransomware actors and other cybercriminals.\25\ 
Garantex's successor entity, Grinex, is itself a vehicle for sanctions 
evasion, as it was created by Garantex employees to move funds after 
Garantex was designated by OFAC for operating in Russia's financial 
services sector.\26\ Following these public designations, MEXC Global 
directly facilitated approximately USD 129 million in activity with 
Garantex and USD 4.1 million in activity with Grinex, and MEXC Global 
continued to transact with both entities as recently as June 2026. 
Similarly, MEXC Global transacted with components of the Russia-based 
A7 Network,\27\ a self-described sanctions-resistant payment service 
provider created by the U.S.-, EU- and UK-designated Moldovan oligarch 
Ilan Shor \28\ and Russia's state-owned defense bank Promsvyazbank 
Public Joint Stock Company (PSB),\29\ that has evolved into a conduit 
for illicit activity associated with a wide range of threat actors, 
including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its Quds 
Force, DPRK-affiliated actors;

[[Page 72423]]

Iran-backed terrorist organizations; and cybercriminals and ransomware 
actors.\30\ Significantly, OFAC has designated the founders and core 
components and enablers of the A7 Network, and recently designated the 
A7 Network, itself, as a significant transnational criminal 
organization.\31\ Further, FinCEN recently found that transactions 
involving any company operating outside of the United States that is 
controlled by the A7 Network belong to a class of transactions of 
primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit 
finance.\32\ Based on analysis of blockchain data, FinCEN assesses that 
MEXC Global facilitated the transmission of at least USD 26 million 
benefitting the now sanctioned A7 Network and sent or received almost 
USD 200 million connected to the A7A5 token (a ruble-backed stablecoin 
that operates on the Tron and Ethereum blockchains \33\ to transfer 
value across A7 Network-linked actors where banking channels are 
restricted or less dependable),\34\ including its issuer Old Vector LLC 
and owner Ilan Shor, both sanctioned by OFAC, as well as the European 
Union and the United Kingdom.\35\

2. MEXC Global Is Used in Furtherance of International Money Laundering
    According to public and non-public information, MEXC Global also 
facilitates activity in furtherance of international money laundering 
in support of Iran and its proxies, financial facilitators of the DPRK, 
and cybercrime.
a. MEXC Global Facilitated Transactions Involving Iran and Its Proxies
    According to FinCEN analysis of blockchain information, between May 
2021 and May 2026, MEXC Global facilitated the transmission of nearly 
USD 2 billion connected to identified Iranian actors or known or 
suspected terrorist groups, including approximately USD 1.87 billion in 
transactions with exposure to Iran, a jurisdiction that is the subject 
of comprehensive U.S. sanctions \37\ and special measures imposed by 
FinCEN pursuant to section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act (31 U.S.C. 5318A) 
which prohibit covered financial institutions from opening or 
maintaining correspondent accounts in the United States for, or on 
behalf of, Iranian financial institutions.\38\ Despite the fact that 
MEXC Global's user agreement states that individuals and entities 
located in Iran are not allowed to use its platform, FinCEN assesses 
that over USD 1 billion of this exposure took the form of direct 
transactions between MEXC Global and more than 40 identified Iranian 
CVC exchangers, some of which are the subject of U.S. and international 
sanctions. Between May 2021 and May 2026, FinCEN assesses that MEXC 
Global also facilitated the transmission of approximately USD 22 
million in transactions associated with the U.S.- and EU-sanctioned 
Central Bank of Iran and the U.S.-, EU-, and UK-sanctioned IRGC and its 
Quds Force.\39\

c. MEXC Global Facilitated Transactions Connected to Cybercrime
    Finally, MEXC Global frequently processes transactions connected to 
cyber-enabled crimes, ranging from darknet marketplace activity 
(including the Russian darknet marketplace activity discussed above) 
and ransomware payments to scam proceeds and stolen funds. Between May 
2021 and May 2026, FinCEN assesses that at least USD 1.99 billion in 
funds originating from or moving to illicit cyber actors moved through 
MEXC Global, an average of more than USD 1 million per day. Between 
January 2022 to July 2024, MEXC Global received more than USD 37.9 
million in suspected ransomware payments, with exposure to over 125 
ransomware variants. MEXC Global also hosts a particularly high-use 
ransomware-related deposit address, which received over USD 1.17 
million during the same period.

C. The Extent to Which MEXC Global Is Used for Legitimate Business 
Purposes

    In reaching its finding that MEXC Global is a financial institution 
operating outside the United States of primary money laundering concern 
in connection with Russian illicit finance, FinCEN considered the 
extent to which MEXC Global is used for legitimate business 
purposes.\44\ As of June 2026, MEXC Global conducted USD 1 billion in 
daily transactions, putting it among the top 20 largest CVC exchangers 
in the world by trading volume. Although FinCEN does not have full 
insight into the scope of MEXC Global's legitimate activities, for the 
purposes of this action, FinCEN assumes that a portion of MEXC Global's 
business activities are legitimate. However, FinCEN assesses that since 
May 2021, MEXC Global has facilitated at least USD 16.7 billion in 
likely illicit activity. Accordingly, any legitimate business conducted 
by MEXC Global is outweighed by the risks posed by MEXC Global's 
facilitation of illicit activity, including sanctions evasion by Russia 
and Iran, and the need to protect the U.S. financial sector from the 
money laundering and terrorist financing risks presented by MEXC 
Global.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \44\ See 31 U.S.C. 5318A(c)(2)(B)(ii).

D. The Extent to Which This Action Would Guard Against International 
Money Laundering and Other Financial Crimes Associated With Russian 
Illicit Finance

    A finding that MEXC Global is of primary money laundering concern 
in connection with Russian illicit finance establishes--and 
emphasizes--the significant illicit finance risks posed by MEXC 
Global's provision of financial services to the Russian illicit finance 
ecosystem, Russian and other darknet markets and high-risk exchanges. 
Further, notwithstanding MEXC Global's ties to Russian illicit finance, 
FinCEN assesses that it has facilitated over USD 1.87 billion in 
transactions with exposure to Iran, including over USD 1 billion in 
direct transactions between MEXC Global and Iranian CVC exchangers, as 
well as transactions benefiting the DPRK and an array of illicit cyber 
actors, each of which present significant risks to the U.S. financial 
system. Accordingly, this order will place U.S. and foreign financial 
institutions and regulators on notice to guard against those risks. 
Moreover, such a finding--in combination with a prohibition on certain 
transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global by covered financial 
institutions--will help safeguard the U.S. financial system by severing 
MEXC Global's access.

IV. Imposition of a Special Measure Prohibiting Certain Transmittals of 
Funds Involving MEXC Global

    Having found that MEXC Global is a financial institution operating 
outside of the United States that is of primary money laundering 
concern in connection with Russian illicit finance, FinCEN has 
determined that the imposition of a special measure prohibiting certain 
transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global is warranted.\45\ In making 
this determination and assessing which special measures may be 
appropriate, FinCEN has considered the relevant evidence in light of 
factors identified in 31 U.S.C. 5318A(a)(4)(B). While FinCEN is under 
no obligation pursuant to section 9714 to consider any particular 
factor or set of factors in selecting one or more special measures, it 
nonetheless finds these factors instructive in guiding the analysis set 
forth below.\46\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

would have a significant adverse systemic impact on the 
international payment, clearance, and settlement system, or on 
legitimate business activities involving the particular 
jurisdiction, institution, class of transactions, or type of 
account; and
    (4) the effect of the action on United States national security 
and foreign policy.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

[[Page 72425]]

A. Whether the Prohibition Would Address the Money Laundering Concern 
in a Manner Consistent With U.S. National Security and Foreign Policy 
Interests

    FinCEN has considered the effect this action will have on U.S. 
national security and foreign policy, as well as the extent to which 
multilateral groups or other nations have taken similar actions.\47\ 
FinCEN has found that, in addition to facilitating Russian illicit 
financial activity and sanctions evasion schemes and serving as a high-
density transactional node for high-risk CVC exchangers, MEXC Global 
plays a broader role in facilitating transactions for a diverse range 
of transnational illicit actors. In particular, MEXC Global processes 
transactions connected to Iranian sanctions evasion, terrorist 
financing, and the laundering of scam and ransomware proceeds. FinCEN, 
therefore, assesses that imposing a prohibition on certain transmittals 
of funds involving MEXC Global is necessary to safeguard U.S. national 
security and the U.S. financial system, as well as to serve key U.S. 
national security objectives.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \47\ See 31 U.S.C. 5318A(a)(4)(B)(i), (iv).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In light of the quantity and volume of transactions linked to known 
or suspected illicit activity processed through MEXC Global, 
prohibiting certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global would 
insulate the U.S. financial system from money laundering and other 
financial crimes. In particular, prohibiting certain transmittals of 
funds involving MEXC Global would further ongoing U.S. efforts to 
curtail suspected Russia-associated illicit activity and financial 
transactions. And, targeting illicit proceeds moved by sanctions 
evasion networks, especially those with a nexus to Iran, is of highest 
priority for the United States. Consequently, prohibiting certain 
transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global will serve the U.S. 
national security and foreign policy interests by protecting the U.S. 
and international financial system from known threat actors.
    Moreover, this action reinforces the expectations of AML/CFT 
compliance in the financial system, highlighting the importance of 
identifying and reporting suspicious activity by financial institutions 
around the world. With respect to the illicit finance risks posed by 
MEXC Global, that is of particular importance, as this order addresses 
primary money laundering concerns that are still ongoing after multiple 
jurisdictions' financial regulators have issued notices highlighting 
that MEXC Global has operated in their jurisdictions without the proper 
license, and in at least one case added the CVC exchanger to a list of 
suspicious CVC trading platforms.\48\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \48\ MEXC Global has been the subject of regulatory scrutiny and 
has been found to be operating without a license in the Seychelles, 
Hong Kong, and Japan. See Financial Services Authority Seychelles, 
Press Release--FSA Takes Enforcement Action Against MX Global Ltd 
for Unlicensed Virtual Asset Services Operations (May 26, 2026), 
https://fsaseychelles.sc/news/press-releases/fsa-takes-enforcement-action-against-mx-global-ltd-for-unlicensed-virtual-asset-services-operations; Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission, SFC Warns 
Public Against Unlicensed Virtual Asset Trading Platform MEXC (Mar. 
15, 2024), https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/news-and-announcements/news/doc?refNo=24PR48; Japanese Financial Services 
Agency, FSA Weekly Review No. 533 (Apr. 13, 2023), https://www.fsa.go.jp/en/newsletter/weekly2023/533.html.
    See Japanese Financial Services Agency, Newsletter, FSA Weekly 
Review No.533 (Apr. 13, 2023), https://www.fsa.go.jp/en/newsletter/weekly2023/533.html.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

B. Whether the Prohibition of Certain Transmittals of Funds Would 
Impose Undue Burdens on Legitimate Activity of MEXC Global or Third 
Parties

    FinCEN has considered whether prohibiting certain transmittals of 
funds would create a significant competitive disadvantage, including 
any undue cost or burden associated with compliance, for financial 
institutions organized or licensed in the United States, as well as the 
extent to which the action could have a significant adverse systemic 
impact on legitimate business activities currently being conducted on 
the MEXC Global platform.\49\ Indeed, while MEXC Global is used by 
licit actors, the legitimate business services that it offers are 
commonly offered by other regulated institutions, meaning that such 
licit actors could readily find alternatives to facilitate business.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \49\ See 31 U.S.C. 5318A(a)(4)(B)(ii), (iii).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    And, FinCEN assesses that prohibiting certain transmittals of funds 
involving MEXC Global will not present a significant competitive 
disadvantage for or put an undue burden on financial institutions 
organized or licensed in the United States. Compliance with the 
prohibition on certain transmittals of funds set out in this order 
requires no tools or competencies other than those already employed by 
domestic financial institutions to maintain their current AML/CFT 
compliance programs. To aid covered U.S. financial institutions with 
compliance, FinCEN has elected to provide within this order for the 
rejection of certain transmittals of CVC that are received from or 
originate at MEXC Global and outline the steps a covered financial 
institution should take in such circumstances. In providing for the 
rejection of CVC under certain limited circumstances, FinCEN 
acknowledges that, at this time, there are technological limitations 
that may limit or preclude covered financial institutions from 
declining CVC transfers originating at addresses outside of their 
control, and compliant institutions may find themselves in receipt of 
CVC from MEXC Global despite a desire and effort to limit such 
exposure.\50\ This order therefore allows covered financial 
institutions the flexibility to act with discretion based on the facts 
and circumstances of a particular transaction and comply with this 
order, even where the originating address is no longer accessible, 
where, for example, (1) CVC transfers originated from MEXC Global, but 
were held for an extended period of time in an unhosted wallet, or (2) 
the covered financial institution's risk mitigation procedures would 
preclude returning funds to MEXC Global. Moreover, by providing for the 
rejection of CVC, this order ensures that covered financial 
institutions will not be subject to an undue cost or burden associated 
with compliance.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \50\ FinCEN notes that CVC payment systems are often designed to 
limit the control of specific financial institutions over 
transactions and to prevent rejection of funds by persons or 
entities other than the sender of funds. As a result, although 
covered financial institutions may institute an internal prohibition 
on the sending of CVC transactions to another address or entity, 
FinCEN assesses that there are few, if any, readily available ways 
for covered financial institutions to ``reject'' incoming CVC 
transactions (prior to receipt).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

C. Whether Any Other Reasonable Alternatives or Special Measures Would 
Adequately Address the Money Laundering Concern

    Before deciding to impose a prohibition on certain transmittals of 
funds, FinCEN considered other available special measures.\51\ After 
due

[[Page 72426]]

consideration, FinCEN has determined that a special measure prohibiting 
certain transmittals of funds involving MEXC Global is the appropriate 
means to adequately address the illicit finance risks posed by MEXC 
Global.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \51\ As noted in section II.A, pursuant to section 9714, these 
measures include: (1) the special measures described in 31 U.S.C. 
5318A(b), including the imposition of additional recordkeeping, 
information collection, and reporting requirements on covered U.S. 
financial institutions and/or the imposition of conditions upon the 
opening or maintaining of correspondent or payable-through accounts 
for or on behalf of a foreign banking institution; and (2) the 
prohibition of, or imposition of conditions on, the transmittal of 
funds.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    None of the special measures set out in 31 U.S.C. 5318A--special 
measures one through five--would effectively address the illicit 
finance threat posed by MEXC Global. Any additional recordkeeping, 
information collection, or reporting requirements, as described in 31 
U.S.C. 5318A(b)(1)-(4), would be insufficient to guard against the 
risks posed by covered financial institutions processing transmittals 
of funds involving MEXC Global. Those special measures would allow such 
transfers to continue to the benefit of illicit actors connected to 
Russian illicit finance, as well as Iran-related and other illicit 
financial activity. Further, merely prohibiting and/or placing 
conditions upon the opening or maintaining in the United States of 
correspondent accounts or payable-through accounts for or on behalf of 
MEXC Global, as described in 31 U.S.C. 5318A(b)(5), would be similarly 
inadequate. Neither prohibiting nor imposing conditions on such 
accounts would safeguard the U.S. financial system to the same degree 
as prohibiting transmittals of funds, as such a special measure would 
not address the movement of funds outside of a strict correspondent or 
payable-through relationship, for example, through the movement of 
funds outside the traditional banking relationship, which may permit 
MEXC Global to access USD through indirect correspondent relationships 
via other foreign financial institutions.

D. Whether the Prohibition Should Be Imposed by Order or Regulation

    Pursuant to section 9714, the Secretary may impose one or more 
special measures, including a prohibition on certain transmittals of 
funds, ``by order, regulation or otherwise as permitted by law.'' In 
determining the appropriate approach in this instance, FinCEN 
considered imposing the prohibition by order or regulation, taking into 
account the nature of the underlying threat, and determined that 
proceeding by an order is the most appropriate course of action given 
the imminent threats posed by the illicit actors whose transactions and 
access to funds MEXC Global facilitates, as well as the ongoing 
transactions associated with suspected activity related to Russian 
illicit finance that continue to be processed through MEXC Global. 
Further, FinCEN has assessed that this order will not be unduly 
burdensome or impose new or unique compliance costs on financial 
institutions.
    A copy of this order will be published in the Federal Register. To 
the extent MEXC Global or other parties have information relevant to 
this order, they may submit it to FinCEN at www.fincen.gov/contact.

V. Executive Order 14294

    Section 5 of Executive Order 14294 directs that all future notices 
of proposed rulemaking (NPRMs) and final rules published in the Federal 
Register, the violation of which may constitute criminal regulatory 
offenses, should include a statement identifying that the rule or 
proposed rule is a criminal regulatory offense and the authorizing 
statute.\52\ Executive Order 14294 directs agencies to draft this 
statement in consultation with the Department of Justice.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \52\ Executive Order 14294, Fighting Overcriminalization in 
Federal Regulations, 90 FR 20367 (issued May 9, 2025; published May 
14, 2025), https://www.federalregister.gov/executive-order/14294.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Executive Order 14294 further directs that the regulatory text of 
all NPRMs and final rules with criminal consequences published in the 
Federal Register after May 9, 2025, should explicitly state a mens rea 
requirement for each element of a criminal regulatory offense, 
accompanied by citations to the relevant provisions of the authorizing 
statute.
    Willful violations of any final regulations set forth in this order 
may be subject to criminal penalties pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 5322 and 
regulations promulgated in 31 CFR Chapter X. The statutory authority 
for criminal liability requires a mens rea of willfulness as an element 
pursuant to 31 U.S.C. 5322(a) and 31 U.S.C. 5322(b). FinCEN's existing 
regulation, 31 CFR 1010.840, that sets out criminal penalties for 
violations of regulations promulgated in 31 CFR Chapter X also includes 
a mens rea of willfulness. In drafting this statement, FinCEN has 
consulted with the Department of Justice.

VI. Order

A. Definitions

1. MEXC Global
    The order defines ``MEXC Global,'' a Seychelles-based CVC 
exchanger, to include its branches, subsidiaries, and offices operating 
as a financial institution in any jurisdiction outside of the United 
States, and any successor entities. For the purposes of this order, a 
successor entity means any person that replaces MEXC Global, its 
branches, subsidiaries, and offices by acquiring its assets, in whole 
or in part, and/or carrying on the affairs of MEXC Global under a new 
name. This includes, but is not limited to, any entities referenced in 
this order as being branches, subsidiaries, or offices of MEXC Global 
operating as a financial institution in any jurisdiction outside of the 
United States. Any branches, subsidiaries, and offices of MEXC Global 
located in the United States are expressly excluded from the definition 
of ``MEXC Global'' for the purposes of this order.
2. Convertible Virtual Currency
    The order defines ``convertible virtual currency'' (CVC) as a 
medium of exchange that either has an equivalent value to currency, or 
acts as a substitute for currency, but lacks legal tender status. 
Bitcoin, despite having legal tender status in at least one 
jurisdiction, is included as a type of CVC for the purpose of this 
order.
3. Covered Financial Institution
    The order defines ``covered financial institution'' as having the 
same meaning as ``financial institution'' in 31 CFR 1010.100(t).
4. Transmittals of Funds
    The order defines ``transmittals of funds'' as the sending and 
receiving of funds, including CVC. For avoidance of doubt, for this 
section, this definition of transmittal of funds applies rather than 
the definition of ``transmittal of funds'' in section 1010.100(ddd).
5. Meaning of Other Terms
    All terms used but not otherwise defined herein shall have the 
meaning set forth in 31 CFR chapter X and 31 U.S.C. 5312.

B. Prohibition on Transmittals of Funds Involving MEXC Global

    A covered financial institution is prohibited from engaging in any 
transmittal of funds from or to MEXC Global.

C. Order Period

    The terms of this order are effective December 10, 2026, with no 
cessation date.

D. Reservation of Authority

    FinCEN reserves authority to impose conditions on certain 
transmittals of funds from or to MEXC Global and to grant appropriate 
exemptions from the requirements of this order.

[[Page 72427]]

E. Other Obligations

    Nothing in this order shall be construed to modify, impair, or 
otherwise affect any requirements or obligations to which a covered 
financial institution is subject pursuant to the BSA, including, but 
not limited to, the filing of Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs), or 
other applicable laws or regulations, such as the sanctions 
administered and enforced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's 
Office of Foreign Assets Control.

F. Penalties for Noncompliance

    The covered financial institution, and any of its officers, 
directors, employees, and agents, may be liable for civil or criminal 
penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322 for willfully violating this 
order.

G. Validity of Order

    Any judicial determination that any provision of this order is 
invalid shall not affect the validity of any other provision of this 
order, and each other provision shall thereafter remain in full force 
and effect.

Jimmy L. Kirby,
Deputy Director, Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.

title: [Proposed Rule] Threshold for the Requirement To Collect, Retain, and Transmit Information on Funds Transfers and Transmittals of Funds That Begin or End Outside the United States, and Clarification of the Requirement To Collect, Retain, and Transmit Information on Transactions Involving Convertible Virtual Currencies and Digital Assets With Legal Tender Status; Withdrawal
abstract: FinCEN and the Board (collectively, the "Agencies") are withdrawing the joint notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) published on October 27, 2020, that proposed modifying the threshold in the Agencies' rules implementing the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) requiring financial institutions to collect and retain information on certain funds transfers and transmittals of funds. The NPRM would have reduced this threshold from $3,000 to $250 for funds transfers and transmittals of funds that begin or end outside the United States. FinCEN additionally proposed reducing from $3,000 to $250 the threshold in FinCEN's rule requiring financial institutions to transmit to other financial institutions in the payment chain information on funds transfers and transmittals of funds that begin or end outside the United States. The NPRM also would have clarified the meaning of "money" as used in the Agencies' rules to specify that the rules apply to domestic and cross-border transactions involving convertible virtual currency (CVC) and digital assets that have legal tender status to a recipient. The Agencies will not take further action on this NPRM.

DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY

Financial Crimes Enforcement Network

31 CFR Parts 1010 and 1020

RIN 1506-AB41


Threshold for the Requirement To Collect, Retain, and Transmit 
Information on Funds Transfers and Transmittals of Funds That Begin or 
End Outside the United States, and Clarification of the Requirement To 
Collect, Retain, and Transmit Information on Transactions Involving 
Convertible Virtual Currencies and Digital Assets With Legal Tender 
Status; Withdrawal

AGENCY: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Treasury; Board 
of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Board).

ACTION: Proposed rule; withdrawal.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: FinCEN and the Board (collectively, the ``Agencies'') are 
withdrawing the joint notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) published on 
October 27, 2020, that proposed modifying the threshold in the 
Agencies' rules implementing the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) requiring 
financial institutions to collect and retain information on certain 
funds transfers and transmittals of funds. The NPRM would have reduced 
this threshold from $3,000 to $250 for funds transfers and transmittals 
of funds that begin or end outside the United States. FinCEN 
additionally proposed reducing from $3,000 to $250 the threshold in 
FinCEN's rule requiring financial institutions to transmit to other 
financial institutions in the payment chain information on funds 
transfers and transmittals of funds that begin or end outside the 
United States. The NPRM also would have clarified the meaning of 
``money'' as used in the Agencies' rules to specify that the rules 
apply to domestic and cross-border transactions involving convertible 
virtual currency (CVC) and digital assets that have legal tender status 
to a recipient. The Agencies will not take further action on this NPRM.

DATES: FinCEN and the Board are withdrawing the NPRM published at 85 FR 
68005 (October 27, 2020), as of November 9, 2026.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: 
    FinCEN: The FinCEN Regulatory Support Section by submitting an 
inquiry at www.fincen.gov/contact.
    Board: Evan Winerman, Deputy Associate General Counsel, (202) 872-
7578, Legal Division, Board of

[[Page 70825]]

Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 20th Street and Constitution 
Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20551. Users of Telecommunication Device for 
Deaf (TDD) only, call (202) 263-4869.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background

    Certain Federal regulations--often referred to as the 
``Recordkeeping Rule'' and ``Travel Rule''--collectively require banks 
and nonbank financial institutions to collect, retain, and transmit 
information on funds transfers and transmittals of funds in amounts of 
$3,000 or more.\1\ The Recordkeeping Rule, which requires banks and 
nonbank financial institutions to collect and retain information 
related to funds transfers and transmittals of funds that begin or end 
outside the United States, is jointly issued by both the Board and 
FinCEN. The Travel Rule, which requires banks and nonbank financial 
institutions to transmit information on funds transfers and 
transmittals of funds that begin or end outside the United States, is 
issued by FinCEN.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ See 31 CFR 1020.410(a), 1010.410(e) (Recordkeeping Rule); 31 
CFR 1010.410(f) (Travel Rule). The Board's Regulation S incorporates 
the substantive requirements of the Recordkeeping Rule. See 12 CFR 
219.23. For additional background on the Recordkeeping Rule and 
Travel Rule, see generally Board and FinCEN, Threshold for the 
Requirement To Collect, Retain, and Transmit Information on Funds 
Transfers and Transmittals of Funds That Begin or End Outside the 
United States, and Clarification of the Requirement To Collect, 
Retain, and Transmit Information on Transactions Involving 
Convertible Virtual Currencies and Digital Assets With Legal Tender 
Status, 85 FR 68005, 68006-07 (Oct. 27, 2020).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    On October 27, 2020, FinCEN and the Board published a joint NPRM 
that proposed modifying the Recordkeeping Rule to reduce the threshold 
at which banks and nonbank financial institutions must collect and 
retain certain information from $3,000 to $250.\2\ FinCEN additionally 
proposed to modify the Travel Rule to change the threshold at which 
banks and nonbank financial institutions must transmit information from 
$3,000 to $250.\3\ The Agencies also proposed clarifying the meaning of 
``money'' in these rules by revising the definitions of ``payment 
order'' and ``transmittal order'' to specify that the Recordkeeping 
Rule and Travel Rule apply to domestic and cross-border transactions 
involving CVC or any digital asset having legal tender status to a 
recipient.\4\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \2\ See 85 FR 68007-10.
    \3\ See id.
    \4\ See 85 FR 68010-11.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

II. Summary of Public Comments

    The Agencies received nearly 3,000 comments on the proposal from 
depository institutions, money services businesses, trade associations, 
individuals, and others.\5\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \5\ A significant majority of these comment letters were 
substantially similar form letters.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Commenters generally opposed the proposal to reduce the thresholds 
applicable to the Recordkeeping Rule and Travel Rule for international 
transactions. Many comments argued that a threshold of $250 would 
impose a significant regulatory burden on financial institutions, 
particularly smaller financial institutions; would disrupt the ability 
of consumers to send remittances overseas (and could potentially drive 
consumers into less regulated marketplaces); would significantly 
increase the number of transactions subject to the provisions of the 
Recordkeeping Rule and Travel Rule; and would increase the liability 
exposure of financial institutions required to maintain personally 
identifiable information. Many comments also noted that some 
potentially illicit transactions under the $3,000 threshold were 
already being reported to FinCEN through Suspicious Activity Reports 
(SARs). A number of commenters asserted that the Agencies did not 
provide sufficient analysis or data to justify the proposed reduction 
in the threshold. Several commenters stated that, rather than decrease 
the threshold, the Agencies should adopt a higher threshold due to the 
effects of inflation since the original threshold was adopted in 1995.
    Commenter sentiment was mixed with respect to the proposal to 
specify that the Recordkeeping Rule and Travel Rule apply to CVC 
transactions. In general, companies that provide CVC-related services 
(and related trade associations) opposed this aspect of the proposal, 
while some depository institutions, money services businesses, and 
related trade associations supported this aspect of the proposal. 
Commenters opposed to this aspect of the proposal stated that 
implementing the proposal would be challenging (e.g., due to 
technological limitations and the lack of an international messaging 
standard for CVC transactions), that the proposal would inhibit CVC 
innovation, and that the Agencies should improve coordination with 
other regulators who were, at that time, simultaneously developing 
rules affecting the CVC industry.
    Many commenters offered more general comments on the proposal, 
including that the proposal would constitute an unwarranted invasion of 
privacy or an unreasonable search and seizure in violation of the 
Fourth Amendment. Many commenters also stated that the comment period 
on the proposal was insufficient, and that, if the Agencies finalize 
the proposal, the proposed implementation period should be extended.

III. Withdrawal of NPRM

    The Agencies have reconsidered the proposal in light of the public 
comments received and have determined to withdraw the joint NPRM for 
two primary reasons. First, more than five years have passed since the 
issuance of the NPRM, and the Agencies believe that additional feedback 
from the public would be useful before the Agencies adopted any 
amendments to the Recordkeeping Rule or Travel Rule that are similar to 
the proposed amendments. The proposal is being withdrawn to provide 
certainty to the public that no final rule will be issued without an 
additional opportunity for public comment.
    Second, and relatedly, the Agencies believe that there have been 
significant recent developments in the CVC industry since the proposal 
was issued. For example, CVC markets have continued to mature, and new 
legal frameworks are emerging.\6\ The Agencies believe that any future, 
potential amendments to the Recordkeeping Rule and Travel Rule related 
to CVC should be considered in light of these recent developments to 
ensure that such amendments are fit for purpose.\7\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \6\ For example, on July 18, 2025, a Federal statute 
establishing a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins was 
enacted. Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. 
Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act, Public Law 119-27; 12 U.S.C. 5901 et seq.
    \7\ See White House, Strengthening American Leadership in 
Digital Financial Technology, p. 100 (July 2025), https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Digital-Assets-Report-EO14178.pdf; see also E.O. 14178, 90 FR 8647 (Jan. 31, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Because the Agencies no longer intend to issue a final rule with 
respect to this proposal, the NPRM published at 85 FR 68005 is hereby 
withdrawn.

Jimmy L. Kirby,
Deputy Director, Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.

    Jointly issued by:

    By order of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve 
System.
Benjamin McDonough,
Secretary of the Board.
